My hon. friend gave me notice yesterday of this question, and in reply I may assure him that the total cash proceeds of the new victory loan will be used for war purposes. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1942, the ordinary expenditures of the government of the Dominion of Canada are estimated at $468,000,000, including $35,000,000 for wheat acreage reductions. The total ordinary revenue is estimated to amount to SI,400,000,000, which means that Canada is raising from current taxation about three times the government's ordinary expenditures.
We are spending more than this great taxation surplus over ordinary expenditures on the war effort; in fact we are spending on direct war effort a total of at least $1,300,000,000. Total expenditures on behalf of Canada are thus at least $1,768,000,000. In addition we are sending vitally needed supplies from Canada to Great Britain, which Great Britain is unable for the time being to pay for with Canadian dollars. This will add approximately $800,000,000 to our burden after deducting the amount of our own exchange deficit with the United States. Our government must provide the Canadian dollars with which to pay our workmen, fanners, miners, transport workers, et cetera, for the cost of producing these supplies which are so urgently needed. Or to put it another way by expressing it in percentages.

speechtext:
I
would like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) if he will be kind enough to give consideration to the following. From the business and commercial standpoint, the city of Toronto at present has no direct representation in the cabinet. This may not be a matter which a private member should bring up, but the Prime Minister's family have had a very long and close association with the public affairs of that city, his grandfather having been its first mayor. The city is the commercial and industrial metropolis of Canada, a leader in war work, recruiting, patriotic activities of all kinds, and a large subscriber to war loans. True, the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) was born and bred there and his distinguished grandfather has done a great deal for the city, but the Postmaster General does not represent a Toronto seat directly, and in the past we have at times had two or three ministers in the cabinet representing the city. Will the Prime Minister give consideration in the contemplated cabinet changes to giving our city increased representation in addition to our present representative?

I have a point in mind
which has reference to sections 1 and 2. I refer to the commitments which have been undertaken by some of the smaller groups who are subject to income tax, and I object to the increases in schedule A as they apply to these groups. Since the budget of 1940, and the taxes enumerated in the schedule appended thereto, many people have made commitments to build houses. I strongly dissent from the opinion expressed yesterday by the hon. member for Parkdale respecting housing in Toronto. As to slums in Toronto we have few now. The public utilities, the civic transportation facilities and good roads have made possible the building of small houses in Toronto and district at small cost.
In my opinion reconsideration should be given to schedule A, for the benefit of workers who have already made contracts for building or buying houses. It is a grave mistake to make jumps in taxes such as are here indicated, and which affect small wage-earners. Their commitments on mortgages and insurance premiums are already burdensome, to say nothing of heavy taxation. We have now in progress a campaign for victory loan subscriptions-and what it will cost, I have no idea. But about 70 per cent of the people in greater Toronto cannot subscribe to it, because of the heavy load I have mentioned, although they are anxious to do their part and subscribe in a small way.

Income War Tax Act
Many of the persons affected are soldiers. If there were a postponement of the payment of mortgage commitments and insurance premiums where they have been regularly paid for years, at the same rate as the victory loan instead of 7 per cent, then they would subscribe. They are anxious to do so, because some of them are serving on victory loan committees. On section 4-Earned income.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Paragraph (m) defines "earned income," and included in the paragraph is the expression "indemnities or other remuneration paid to members of dominion, provincial or territorial legislative bodies or municipal councils." By express direction the indemnities paid to members of parliament are included in the category of salaries and wages. I dissent from that principle. I do not wish it to be understood that I am arguing for exemption from national taxation, either with regard to income tax or national defence tax, as they apply to the indemnities paid to members of parliament. That is not so at all. I say that from the very beginning, from away back in 1917, members of parliament have been glad to pay the imposts levied upon their indemnities. My objection is that the paragraph is based on an improper and unconstitutional theory. Indemnities are not wages paid to members of parliament. They are, in fact, indemnities, as indicated in the act under which they are paid. Therefore I say it is wrong in principle to tax, as salaries or wages either for income or national defence tax purposes, the indemnities of members of parliament. But in order to keep the position absolutely straight I suggest the ministry should follow the principle enunciated when salary deductions were made in 1931. At that time members of parliament were the first people in the public service to take the deduction of 10 per cent on their indemnities. It was done on the theory that the crown would be authorized so to do by the people's elected representatives, who are not employees of the crown;
they voluntarily relinquished 10 per cent of their indemnities for the good of the country.
I suggest therefore that the minister should correct the position indicated in this paragraph. He should maintain the constitutional position of members of parliament, and should take the authority, which will be given with the greatest good-will by members of the House of Commons, and, I am sure, of the other place, to put into effect what I conceive to be the correct constitutional principle. If part of these indemnities is to be allocated to the service of the state, then I suggest that it be done by way of a bill to deduct from the indemnities of members of parliament the income and national defence taxes applicable. But the indemnities ought not to be taxed on the theory that members of parliament are employees of the crown.
I expressly repudiate the suggestion contained in the Income War Tax Act that we are in any sense the employees of the crown. If one were to carry that a little farther he would reach the logical conclusion that we are also employees of the present government, and I expressly dissent from that idea. I am satisfied that if any private member thinks the matter through, and studies the constitutional aspect of the question he will agree that we are the representatives of the people under the constitution, and we are not here as employees of any government, no matter what its political stripe may be. This is a question of principle. It is not a matter of great consequence from the point of view of dollars and cents; that is not the point at all. But to say that we are employees of the crown is a false doctrine and we should not for a moment tolerate it in any legislation on the statute books.
I suggest to the minister that even if it is late in the session he consider adopting the principle that the taxation of members of parliament should be on the theory, not that we are employees of the government or of the crown, but that we are the elected representatives of the people and that we voluntarily submit to a deduction from that indemnity which parliament in days gone by saw fit to grant to us. That is the principle I am contending for. Simply by putting a clause in an act of parliament you cannot make me an employee of the crown. That is not the principle of democratic government. That is hoisting yourself by your boot-straps; it is saying that black is white.
We all agree that we should be taxed. No one for a moment has offered the suggestion that we should not be taxed as other people are. In fact we desire to set an example to the rest of the public in bearing our fair share of taxation, but let us put it on the
Income War Tax Act

proper principle and not on a theory that is false in fact and false under the constitution of the country.
Mr. O'BRIEN: In view of the fact that I raised this question when the matter was in the resolution stage, I am pleased that the leader of the opposition has presented the same view to the committee and has substantiated my remarks. Therefore I have nothing more to say except to ask the minister to see that the anomaly is corrected, as the leader of the opposition has urged. Parliament had the power to legislate as it did in regard to this matter, but when parliament did so it committed constitutional suicide, and I submit that we should now take our position once more on firm ground.

Earned income, as defined by section 4, is not earned income at all; in some cases not half of what can be classed as income is ever received by the earner when you allow for deductions that have to be made by the person earning it. The new income tax principle is very unfair. One of the main provisions is section 4 which gives the definition according to the officials. While I have great admiration for these officials, I submit that it is the function and the duty of parliament to revise these clauses. Under the law to-day, all that we can do is to perform a postmortem, because we cannot change one word of Bill No. 87. Not one word can be altered by the representatives of the people, who are responsible to them for this bill. In Washington it is different. There they discussed income tax and revenues for months before the budget of the secretary of the treasury, Mr. Morgenthau, was adopted; they can make any changes they like. If we cannot make any changes we may as well pass the bill holus bolus and take the definition of earned income given us, which means salaries, wages, fees, bonuses, pensions, superannuation allowances, retiring allowances, gratuities, honoraria, and the income from any office or employment of profit held by any person, and so on. In some cases under this section as much as fifty per cent of the earnings from these sources has been taken away, and the earner does not get it at all, yet he has to pay on the full sum, not the net. Our system of taxation is most unfair. It is robbing Peter to pay Paul. I am in favour of income tax and always have been, but I believe the principle of this section giving the definition of earned income is unfair. The same is true of the section with regard to investment income. Certainly some part of it should be allowed for deductions now not considered in the matter.

Now that this matter has
been introduced I would call the attention of the committee to another aspect of it. With very few exceptions, I believe, we all agree that income tax is a fair tax. Provided I get an income I am willing to pay a tax on it, whether that tax be large or small; but I do object, and I believe other members will share my view, to being taxed on income which is not received. Many years ago the then minister of finance put an amendment into the act-I have not got it before me now-expressly stating in so many words that if a person is away from home in the pursuit of his business and incurs any expense in connection with travelling, or board and lodging, he is entitled to deduct that sum from the gross profits of his business, in the same way that you are allowed to deduct the wages of people you employ. But when it comes to members of parliament that principle is not employed. We are taxed on the full amount of $4,000. Does any member suggest that he gets $4,000 net indemnity? The idea is ridiculous. I employ a stenographer at home solely in connection with political work, and I have other expenses while travelling in the district. If I were running a store I would be allowed to deduct those expenditures, but because I am a member of parliament they are not allowed.
The language used is "business or occupation''. A number of years ago I took this up with the proper official and he said I was not eligible to deduct anything whatever because my status was neither that of a business nor that of an occupation. I asked him if he would tell me what it was if it were neither of these, and he said it was an honour. But you cannot live on an honour. The province of British Columbia does allow a certain amount to be taken off. It used to be $2,000. One was allowed to deduct that, just as a man running a blacksmith's shop is allowed to take off expenses. Later on the province reduced that allowance. It was a flat rate and did not go into details; it simply said $2,000. Since then they have reduced it to $1,000. That is an admission of the principle of the thing. We are no longer able to obtain that reduction there because income tax has been surrendered in that province.
I would not have brought this matter up because it might look as if we were trying to get something for ourselves. Now that it has been brought up, however, it is only right, to point out to the Minister of Finance that we should be allowed either a flat rate or such an amount as we can substantiate without anj' shadow of doubt as expenses incurred in discharging our duties.

Income War Tax Act
as members of parliament. It is not only the amount of indemnity that is involved, but if you have private means added to the indemnity that puts the rate into higher brackets, which increases the tax paid. Tax us all you like on a percentage basis, but do not tax us on something we never get or see. Tax us on our net income from being a member of parliament the same as you would tax us on the net income from being a storekeeper or anything else.
I concur in the view taken by the leader of the opposition, but that is on a somewhat different line. I suggest that we should be allowed either a flat rate in consideration of expenses incurred in obtaining this income, or else a certain amount by vouchers submitted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition objects to having indemnities classed as earnings of an employee. I do not think they are so taxed. The section before the committee, 4(m), contains an exhaustive definition of "earned income"; it enumerates various varieties of earned income or what the act shall consider as earned income. It does not purport to bring them all under the heading of income of employees. The first few lines seem to relate to salaries, wages, fees, bonuses and so on, but it contains such words as "pensions, superannuation allowances, retiring allowances, gratuities, honoraria", and so forth. The middle part of the section is still farther away from any idea of wages or income of an employee, because it deals with the earnings which a person derives from the exercise of his trade, vocation or calling, and then finally the latter part of the section makes it clear that the definition extends to "indemnities or other remuneration paid to members of the dominion, provincial or territorial legislative bodies or municipal councils". I am unable, therefore, to appreciate the argument that in some way the indemnities are being branded as wages or salaries paid by the government to employees of the crown. I do not think that is so. They are simply swept within the definition of earned income, but without any legislative expression of opinion as to whether they are in the nature of wages of employees or not. There is no implication that they are that I can read into this section.
With respect to the argument of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, there is much to be said for it. It is very hard to know just where to draw the line between living expenses which can be allowed as deductions from gross income for income tax purposes and living expenses that should not be so allowed. Parliament, in its wisdom or otherwise, has decided that the travelling expenses, inch ling
meals and lodging of persons travelling in connection with their trade or business-
Or occupation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -while away from home in pursuit of a trade or business, shall be permitted as deductions. But of course it is a principle that should not apply generally. It could not, for example, be applied to a person who is working at home. He has lodging and living expenses, but it would never do to permit him to deduct those from income for income tax purposes, because the income tax is upon the income which he receives for the purpose, among other things, of meeting his living expenses. As I say, it is hard to know where to draw the line. It has always been the law since the inception of the income war tax act that sessional indemnities are income and taxable as income, and that no deduction is allowed for the cost of meals and room in Ottawa any more than deduction in respect of living expenses is allowed for the great mass of the population of the country.
And what about travelling?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Travelling expenses are pretty well provided for by statute. The statute provides a fairly generous allowance for travelling expenses, at least for one trip here and one trip back.
Whatever the abstract or theoretical rights in the controversy may be, it would be thoroughly impracticable for us and undesirable to make any change of this kind at the present time or under existing conditions.

I should like to refer to a paragraph of a letter I received from an official of the national revenue department dated July 29, 1940, when I asked a question last year for information. He says:
As the elected representative of the people in the constituency of Northumberland, New Brunswick, you receive an "indemnity" which is paid by the dominion government. Under the definition of "employee" referred to above you are therefore an employee of the dominion government and as such you personally should file two copies of form N.D.T.l with the representative of the treasury, House of Commons, Ottawa, so that the proper amount of national defence tax may be deducted from the moneys payable to you.
Therefore there seems to be a difference of opinion between the Minister of Finance and the Department of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From whom did the letter
come? Is it the local office?

No.
-Mr. ILSLEY: The dominion office?

Yes.

The Minister of Finance has taken a very narrow view of the argument I used, in confining it to meals and hotel. There are other expenses such as I enumerated, the cost of a stenographer and so forth; and as regards travelling he has surely forgotten the days before he was a cabinet minister when he talks about the expenses being fully or even reasonably met by the allowance to come to Ottawa once a year. I suppose my travelling expenses in covering my district throughout the year will reach $300 or $400, apart from coming to Ottawa, and surely he would not say that is amply provided for. That is hardly the position.
As regards all other income, you pay on your net income, not the gross. You are allowed to take off the cost of obtaining the income, and part of the cost of obtaining this income, or wage if you choose to put it on that low plane, is what I have spoken of.
Running all through the argument of the Minister of Finance on these bills, and apparently a prominent consideration in the minds of his advisers seems to be the trouble of administration. If it is easy to administer, slam it on; if it involves a little trouble, avoid it.	.
British Columbia finds a way of dealing with this. For many years they put a flat rate on; they used to allow us $2,000 a year in recognition of the cost of being a member of the dominion parliament, and then we paid income tax in the province on the remaining $2,000. They have since reduced that to $1,000, and now it will disappear altogether. A flat rate is a simple way of doing it, and it would be a recognition of the situation. I remember hearing Mr. Bennett say in this house that he paid his income tax gladly. I would hardly go so far as that. I pay it willingly, but I do not like paying income tax on something which is not income. I believe we should pay on net instead of on gross remuneration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I can
hardly go as far as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I do not think I should ask the government to allow a deduction for the food I eat; but certainly there is a principle involved in connection with the indemnity of a member of parliament. Certainly he has to incur out of pocket expenditures that he would not incur if he were not a member of parliament. I am not going to labour the point; the hon. member has made out a good case and the minister has recognized that there is something in it, so that perhaps before another session something may be done.
fMr O'Brien.]
At the risk of incurring the indignation of hon. members who want to get this bill through I want to return for a moment to the other point. I object to being classed as an employee. It is true that under a technical construction of this act we are not declared expressly to be employees and therefore with earned income, but we are put in the same category, and that is not the theory of representative government in Canada. I suggest to the minister that we let it go for this year, but that between now and next session he give consideration to a recognition of the true position of a member of parliament, that he is here as a representative of the people under constitutional authority. He gets an indemnity against the loss that he sustains by coming here, and for other things of the kind; and we might be taxed by way of deduction from that indemnity just the same as the judges were taxed in 1931. Some of them, though not many, took the view that there was a contract in connection with their appointment and that therefore they should not be required to pay income tax. Parliament said, "All right; we will recognize the principle of that position, but we are going to deduct from the salary paid you by the crown 10 per cent as a contribution to the state." That was in a time of economic warfare. I am not sure just what the position is with respect to judges to-day; I have not looked it up, but I think there is some tax on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are subject to the payment of income tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On the theory that it is a salary to an employee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The difficulty in connection with judges, under Mr. Bennett, was this. Mr. Bennett objected to reducing their salaries because he felt they should not be subject to reduction, and he held the same view with regard to the salaries of officers and men in the armed forces. There was much to be said for that view, but on the other hand it appeared unfair to reduce the salaries of civil servants and the indemnities of members of parliament by 10 per cent, as was done, and at the same time leave the judges and those in the armed forces untouched. The constitutional position, or something akin to it, was preserved by another plan. A tax of 10 per cent was imposed on the salaries of judges and those in the armed forces, so that it could be said that their salaries having been given them for life, and the independence of the judiciary being extremely important, their salaries had not been reduced, but they were being asked to pay a tax.

In view of the statement of the minister that he cannot see his way clear to consider the point I have raised, I would ask whether he would be in favour of withdrawing the allowance of $2,000 a year given each cabinet minister in lieu of an automobile?

I think it is highly relevant and clearly a case in point, involving your car versus my car.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It may not be quite relevant, but this matter crops up from time to time and we might as well face the situation first as last. What was the position? Prior to the institution of this grant of $2,000 a year to cabinet ministers and the leader of the opposition, ministers of the crown were supplied free of charge with luxurious motor cars, and all kinds of expenses were incurred until it was felt that the cost to the country was exorbitant. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni says it was a scandal. Perhaps that is too broad a term to use generally, but I do think perhaps it approximates the position in certain instances.
Because of that fact it was determined to set up a new position. It was recognized that cabinet ministers and the leader of the opposition of the day-my right hon. friend the Prime Minister occupying that position at the time-should not be supplied at the public expense with a new motor car every year or every second year, with chauffeurs paid by the government, gasoline and oil bought by the government and all that sort of thing, but that they should be given a lump sum in lieu of the amount which had been expended in this way prior to that time. That was done, and I am satisfied that a decided saving to the treasury resulted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am sure there was a decided saving to the treasury, and the minister agrees with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have always understood there was a saving.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have no doubt about it. It would take quite a lot of trouble to demonstrate it mathematically, but I am quite sure it could be done. I recall the instance of a Speaker of this house who got practically a new car by way of repairs, and it was charged up to the government. I am not going to go beyond that, but that sort of thing did develop in isolated cases. I would not have anyone think I believe it was general, but in some instances it did develop into something approaching a scandal.
What is the position to-day? Cabinet ministers and the leader of the opposition are voted by statute the sum of $166.66 per month in lieu of a motor car. What does that mean? If you have not a motor car it means that you absorb it into your general income, which I do not think is right. But if you have a motor car; if you keep a chauffeur; if, as in my position, you have to rent a garage or garage space, you have nothing left. I have kept an account of this thing, and I know that I am distinctly out of pocket. If I did not receive this allowance I would not maintain a car in Ottawa, and I think I would be better off. Then when I went home I would drive my own car, as other people do. Let us be fair about this thing. This is intended to expedite the business of cabinet ministers and the leader of the opposition, and to do away with a position which to say the least was not satisfactory. If it is the desire of the House of Commons in war time that this allowance should not be made, I should be very glad to hear it. Then I would at once dispense with the services of my chauffeur and send my car home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the way I feel about it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But if it is the will of parliament that the Prime Minister of this country should have a motor car at the expense of the country-and I believe he should, or that he should have an allowance in lieu thereof-or that the Minister of National Defence, who has to travel a great deal, should have a car, or any of the other ministers, then I think this is a fair way of doing it. The Leader of the Opposition also has a position that requires him to travel a good deal, and in these cases I do not think it unfair to ask the country to make the contribution. If you pay a chauffeur $25 a week; if you pay your garage rent; if you pay the ordinary cost of maintenance, repairs and so on, you find that $2,000 does not begin to cover the expense, and you have nothing left for the depreciation of your car.
I think I have made a fair statement of the matter, and I hope hon. members will understand my position. So far as I am concerned, I am in the hands of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think perhaps I can explain it. There is some bond interest which is payable either in Canadian or in foreign funds. The provision first was that if a resident of Canada elected to take his interest in a foreign currency which was at a premium he would be subject to a 5 per cent tax. Certain debtors evaded that provision.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Suppose the foreign currency was at a 10 per cent premium, for example. If the bond interest was payable in United States or Canadian currency at the option of the holder, and he elected to be paid in United States currency, he would have the right to be paid the equivalent of $110 Canadian dollars although the coupon was for only $100. Certain debtors worked out this technique. They said to their creditors, "Do not exercise your option and require payment in United States funds but ask us instead for $104.50 in Canadian funds and we will pay that to you".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That was the approach from the debtor company to the coupon holder?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. Municipalities did it largely. The result was that the creditor was just as well off, the debtor was about $5.50 better off on the coupon, and the dominion government was out its tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand the position. How does this correct it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A year or two ago we made a change in the section which was as I have described it, and the amendment provided that if the debtor had the right to require payment at his option in a currency which was at a premium, then the tax attached.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Even if the option was not exercised?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. That was ample protection for the crown, but it was interfering in cases where the debtors had defaulted in whole or in part. So that this is our third attempt at legislation on the subject.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not wish to delay the committee, but since we had the discussion and the minister was good enough to make the change with respect to businesses, leaving the individual returns to be made on March 31, I have received a great many letters on this subject to the effect that the experience of business men in filing their returns is that there is a difficulty on account of the lack of chartered accountants, just as there is a difficulty for the unincorporated company which has to employ chartered accountants. There is a great deal to be said in that regard. For years the public has been used to April 30 and has made plans accordingly. Now a month has been taken off and a protest is made on behalf of certain individuals. I therefore promised to bring the matter up again at this stage.
I am not sure that the minister made it clear why the department desired this change in the first instance. Was it to get the money in early? I do not think that is really a sound reason. Was it because of the great increase in the number of returns to be filed? I do not think that can be a reason, because there are twelve months in the year and just so many hours in the day to do the work. What was the reason for moving it forward a montn in the first instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was considered that three months would give ample time normally for a person to compute his income for the preceding year and make his return. We have provided for four months for businesses, whether incorporated or unincorporated. It brings the money in earlier, yes. That was a consideration. Then we are proposing a scheme for payment by instalments, and this is about the middle of the period.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: For this year, but you have seven months if you start under the new scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are six months
altogether. The first payment is made in September, but the interval between the first payment and March 31 is six months- October to March, both inclusive. In consideration of the taxpayer paying in advance, which would be equivalent to paying half of the income tax three months in advance, he

Income War Tax Act
is allowed to go on paying by instalments for six months after March without interest for the months from April to September inclusive.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Those of us who have adopted the present system of eight payments beginning in January will have concluded our payments, we hope, by the end of August. That will leave four months out of this calendar year, but we are confronted with the tax on this year's income payable next year, and we are given the option of four payments this year, September, October, November and December. We have three months in which to file the returns under this proposal, so that we must reckon our tax, if we are to take advantage of the scheme, as soon as possible after the end of the year and then pay a fraction of the tax as we estimate it ourselves. I think the minister has given the correct reason; I do not think the question of getting the money in is so important. It is just this-I use the word without being offensive-this bureaucracy has decided that it wants the returns filed one month sooner, without regard to the convenience of the taxpayers. That is the bald, naked truth. I do not think parliament should do this just because the officials of the department say they want it. The minister has to give us a better reason than that. Three months may be sufficient for the simple tax return; three months in a given case may not be time enough. I know that if a man makes a pro forma return and a substantial payment he is given consideration, and many a man is grateful for that; I know of cases. And that just has to be; sometimes it is not humanly possible to make the return.
I am not yet convinced that we should make this change. The minister receded in the one case; I ask him to recede in the other and to leave the date April 30. I do not think it will at all affect his programme of partial payments of 1941 income tax payable in 1942.

In making an income tax return for 1941 under the present set-up it is taken for granted one can anticipate in September, October, November and December what his income will be in the last quarter of the year. In starting to make payments in September one does the government a favour by giving it the use of that money six or seven months prior to the time he is obligated to pay it. In recompense for the favour that the taxpayer does the country the government does him the disfavour of cutting the time down one month, saying "You must pay it thirty days ahead because you never did a favour for us before in that particular regard." I do not know whether
the end of the fiscal year being at the end of March has anything to do with the government's desire to have the return made at the end of March. It may have. But the Easter holidays come along usually in April, and there are plenty of people who take advantage perhaps of a few days off at that time to make out their income tax return.
I do not think the advantage that will accrue to the government by having the return made by March 30 outweighs the disadvantage that there will be to the taxpayer, and after all the taxpayer should be given some consideration. Let us not get into the state of mind that we can say, just because the government runs the business of this country and wants this, we are going to be regimented to the extent that the taxpayer has no more rights. That would be a bad state of things for this country to get into. People pay their income tax willingly, they want to make honest returns and within the prescribed time, but the government is doing no great favour to them in giving them a little latitude in the matter of the date of filing the return.

As one who associated himself with the thought expressed by the leader of the opposition in reference to the shortening of the time for filing the return, particularly as applying to unincorporated business firms, I can see that there are advantages as well as disadvantages in connection with it. I am wondering whether the minister had in mind in providing for returns from certain types of income tax payers by March 31 that he was doing the individual a favour. The larger firms, incorporated as well as unincorporated, are able to procure the services of auditors to prepare their accounts, and their time would be taken up to a large extent in the month of April. Anyone's experience in trying to procure their services is that we all wait until the last month to prepare our income tax returns or to check them. We have made a tentative balance sheet and it is then that we find it difficult to obtain the services of auditors. It is just possible that the minister had in mind that thought- greater efficiency so far as the department is concerned, and also making it easier for the individual to procure the professional help he must sometimes have in order to make a correct return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The leader of the opposition says this is what the bureaucracy want.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is the reason the minister gave.
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh no; that was not the reason at all. This term "bureaucracy" is used good-naturedly, but I think it is a shame to be using it too much, because it builds up the idea that there is a group of public enemies here in Ottawa setting their hands and faces against the people of this country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Oh, well; I think I qualified it sufficiently. I do not mean that at all. I will withdraw the term if it is offensive; I certainly had no such idea in mind. I shall say, then, the "permanent officials" want this done. That is the correct description. And I suggest that that is not a good enough reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not the reason I gave, and moreover they do not all want it done either, if that is any satisfaction to the committee. However, I have to take responsibility for these measures, and the tendency to go back and say that this is what some bureaucrats of some kind want may be all very well occasionally, but I do not want the impression to be given that there is a group of civil servants who do not care anything about the convenience or interests of the people. They are doing a very important job and doing it well. I have often heard hon. gentlemen say that myself.
Our present system of instalments ceases in August. That is the plan that is under way now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is last year's plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The eight-months plan. Now it is desirable to get the new system operating in September, and it is more desirable to have the date of payment approximately in the middle of that period than pretty well to the end, especially as there is no reason why it should not be. We are talking about individuals now. My income tax returns are not difficult to make, but I can make them just as well in January as in February or March; I do not need to wait until April, and I think that is true of the overwhelming majority of personal income tax payers.
The hon. member for Renfrew South says we are asking those who are paying on the new instalment plan to estimate their income for the present year. That is not the scheme. The scheme is that they pay on the basis of their last year's income for the months of September to December.
That is estimating.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, they know what their
last year's income was.
But you are estimating it for this year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What the hon. member said was true of last year; you had to estimate it before the end of the fiscal year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Last year, under the scheme for payment in eight instalments, there was very little difficulty because an estimate could be made in January. An estimate cannot be made in September, nor do we ask anyone to do that. We are asking taxpayers to pay for September, October, November and December, on the basis of the income for the previous year.

Anticipating that the
income will not be lower in the succeeding year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; there is no such theory at all. It is in January that the matter is adjusted and spread over the next eight months on such a basis that the whole of the income tax will be paid at the end of the twelve months period. No one is expected to proceed on the assumption that the income for 1941 will be the same as it was for 1940, or for that matter that the income tax will be the same. The one difficulty about changing this date to April 30 is that all our estimates have been based upon this amount coming into the treasury in March, and I do not think it would be worth while to upset everything by giving an extension for that one month. I do not think there is any real inconvenience here.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In individual cases I believe there would be some inconvenience, but I would be inclined to think that such cases would be in the minority, as the minister has indicated. The consideration to which he has just alluded, namely, that it is intended to get in this money in this fiscal year, would be a factor; and I am sorry that this argument was not advanced at an earlier stage in order that we might see what were its implications. It would have the effect of bringing into this fiscal year a very large sum of money, but of course that would flatten out in succeeding years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
However, I am not going to press the matter any further. I have stated the objection on behalf of those interested; the minister will not accept the suggestion, and so far as I am concerned that is the end of it.

Income War Tax Act

I think this change in date, which has been recommended by the departmental officials, is most unfortunate, because the people will not have finished paying their coal bills by the time all these documents must be again prepared and signed. In the recess the minister should endeavour to see if some arrangement cannot be worked out under which all the papers and documents in connection -with municipal and provincial taxation would not be made at the same date, and returns would not come due in the very same month to be filled out and returned just when that has also to be done in connection with federal taxation. Such timing all at once is bad. It is unfortunate also that the timing has not been better arranged in connection with other matters, notably the victory loan now under way. I do not think that should have been brought on while this matter of heavier income taxes was being discussed. The timing is all wrong, and it injures the work of the department generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With the consent of the committee I should like to make a statement about an income tax matter, perhaps not a very large one, that is not strictly relevant to this resolution. I wish the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) were here, but since I am not going to say anything unfavourable to him perhaps his absence does not make very much difference.
Some days ago the hon. member made the statement in the house that some dollnr-a-year man, I think he said in British Columbia, had been making certain expenditures, and he asked me if those expenditures would be allowed as deductions for income tax and excess profits tax purposes. Shortly after that Mr. H. R. MacMillan wired me as follows:
While absent here in connection with shipbuilding I observe in yesterday's papers reports ot discussions in the House of Commons yesterday indicating that an unnamed dollar a year lumberman from British Columbia has built extravagant office building as a means of evading excess profits taxes. It is generally believed here that this discussion in the House of Commons refers to me and to the British Columbia Plywoods Limited a manufacturing company of which I am president. The building referred to was completed in May nineteen thirty-eight. It cost eleven thousand dollars which was charged to capital expenditure. Therefore it not only antedated excess profits taxation but it also in no way evaded any taxation. The circulation in such a prominent manner of such innuendoes undermines confidence in people and in institutions and adversely affects the public morale. Therefore I respectfully ask that you make these facts public.
After I received this telegram I made inquiries and found that it would be strictly
out of order for any hon. member to make an explanation of this sort on the orders of the day, so I left the matter until in committee of the whole I might be able to read the telegram. I did not have any idea of the identity of the person referred to in this house; it may be that the hon. member for Fraser Valley did not refer to Mr. MacMillan, but apparently the newspapers in British Columbia identified Mr. MacMillan as the person referred to, and since he is a valued employee of the government at the present time, and also because of considerations of justice, I thought it desirable to read his telegram.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I concur
in what the minister has done. I think it was quite apparent to those of us who heard the statement that the hon. member for Fraser Valley did refer to Mr. H. R. MacMillan. If the facts are as stated in Mr. MacMillan's telegram, which I do not doubt for a moment, then of course this is just another illustration of gossip being enlarged as it is repeated time and again. You can never catch up with a story like that; there always will be people who will think that what was alleged actually took place. I think the minister has done nothing more than justice to Mr. MacMillan in making this statement.

Sections 24 to 28 inclusive agreed to.
On section 29-Machinery or equipment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the implication of this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Two or three years ago we provided an income tax credit for capital expenditures made by taxpayers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What was the theory? That was before the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. It was done to stimulate employment. Questions have arisen as to what expenditures should come within the meaning of the section. Specifically I mention rolling stock, buses, trucks and certain items of plant not affixed to the soil. It was claimed that these should qualify for the benefit of the section. The section itself is not clear on that and it may be that the courts would hold one way or the other. The memoranda which have been issued made the matter quite clear and this is for the purpose of making it clear in the legislation that machinery or equipment referred to in the
Income War Tax Act

section shall mean only such machinery or equipment as it required to be and is affixed for a permanency within the said period to the business premises of the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is
covered by section 90, part XIV.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. That is a brief
explanation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This
crystallizes into legislation the practice of the department so that it will defeat any attempt to make claims which it was not intended should be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is correct. It never was intended by the department, but it is always questionable what parliament did intend and that is for the courts to say.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Capital
costs were not specifically limited to machinery and fixtures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is arguable. The
section reads:
The capital costs on which the ten per centum shall be calculated are those costs incurred and paid by the taxpayer in the period beginning the first day of May, 1939, and ending the thirtieth day of April, 1940, in respect of work actually done in Canada during the said period, on the construction, manufacture, installation, betterment, replacement, or extension of buildings, machinery or equipment in the said period from the first day of May, 1939, to the thirtieth day of April, 1940, provided such buildings, machinery or equipment are to be used in the earning of the income of the taxpayer.
I believe the intention of the minister and of the department was that these should be permanent installations. The object of the section was to make work, it was to do away with unemployment. A typical case would be where a 'factory owner added an extension to his factory and brought in and fixed machinery to the premises and proceeded to employ help. The work expended on the extension of the plant and so on was what was contemplated by this provision.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It was
aever intended to apply to a new motor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be an extreme case. Some machinery would have to be imported because one could not draw a distinction between that and machinery bought in Canada. However, it was always felt that it was going too far to extend this to movables and so on that were bought.

Sometimes a piece of
heavy machinery gives employment to many men, but at other times it is not necessary to have a large piece of machinery in order to

provide employment. In my county is a man who carries on an interesting trade, the roasting of peanuts and the frying of chips. The only machinery suitable for this work is made in the United States. He has gone to considerable trouble, and I do not know if he has succeeded in getting the foreign exchange control board to permit him to spend $25 in order to buy two machines which will give work to three or four more people during the summer season. This may be considered an unimportant matter, but nothing is unimportant which gives work to people, and from.that point of view even the smallest thing should not be overlooked. In this particular case $25 of Canadian money sent to the United States would have enabled a machine to be imported which is not made here and would have given work to three or four people during the whole summer season. It should not be necessaiy to write several letters in regard to such a matter. Actually four people are employed, but the machine would mean eight people employed, which would mean more salaries and wages.
I would ask the minister to give definite instructions to the foreign exchange control board not to split hairs but to be reasonable when proper requests are made to them. Even if they do not understand the question that is submitted to them they should accept in good faith what is said by those who know more than they ever did in these matters.

Not having the statute before me I would ask the minister what is 'the significance of this addition to subsection 2 of section 90, and what is the significance of the words, "said period" in the second last line of the clause to be added?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The period referred to is
the twelve-months period beginning May 1, 1939, and ending April 30, 1940. Section 90 provides that a certain proportion of certain capital expenditures may during that period be deducted from the income tax payable for that period.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The period has not been extended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And it is taken care of over a period of time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, income tax credits are given over three years, if I remember correctly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: One-third of the 10 per cent each year.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 30-To whom applicable.
Mr. O'BRIEN:	On May 15 when this
legislation was in the resolution stage I asked the minister whether he could define the position of piece-workers as against wage-earners. I will quote from Hansard in order to present the matter in sequence:
Mr. O'Brien:	Before six o'clock I spoke
privately to the minister, asking him to clarify the situation with respect to the tax as it affects the piece-worker. In the lumbering industry of New Brunswick, and I have no doubt in other provinces we have men working by the month on piece-work.
That sentence should as a matter of fact read "we have men working by the month and/or on piece-work." I continue the quotation :
They are paid by the cord. No doubt men in munitions and other plants are paid on a similar piece-work basis. Will the minister tell us if the tax should be deducted by the employer, or are such men treated as contractors?
Mr. Usley: If the piece-worker is an employee, the tax should be deducted. If he is an independent contractor, it should not. In that event he should make a return.
Mr. O'Brien: How would we know whether he is or is not? Does the law give any definition?
Mr. Usley:	Yes. It is just one of those
things which must be decided by the employer himself. It is a very mild legal question, but not one about which it would be necessary to consult a solicitor.
Since the matter is of the utmost importance in the province and in the particular constituency from which I come, as also across Canada, I thought that a more exact definition would be possible and so I wrote to the Department of National Revenue. I quote one paragraph from their letter addressed to me in reply, dated Ottawa, May 19, 1941:
Replying to your letter of the 16th instant you are advised that as piece-workers are regarded as employees for purposes of national defence tax a deduction for such tax is required to be made at the source in all instances where the employee's remuneration exceeds the amounts stipulated in ruling 48 on page 15 of the enclosed brochure.
I wished to have that put on Hansard so that it will be on record and the members of the house and the country generally will understand what tax is to be deducted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In the
case of piece-workers where the relationship of master and servant does not subsist, there is not an employer within the meaning of the statute. But if there is a power of dismissal as distinguished from the power of cancellation of a contract, there would be an employee. I should like to have that distinction 14873-216
made clear. In certain places in New Brunswick in the lumbering business a contract is given to a man to fell logs and yard them at so much per thousand feet, we will say. The man and his family may do all the work, and he is paid at the rate of so much per thousand feet. But there is always retained the power to cancel the contract if he is not proceeding satisfactorily. In most cases he cannot be dismissed, and there the relationship of master and servant does not subsist. I think that must be the test, and I think the department should take that stand. If a man may be dismissed and his service terminated the tax would be exigible. If there is no power of dismissal but only power to cancel the contract-there is a clear distinction-the tax would not be exigible. Most of these cases are of the kind I suggest, namely, piece-work at so much a piece for pit-props or so much a cord for pulpwood. The man is not hired in the ordinary sense of master and servant, but the right of cancellation is retained if the man's work is not satisfactory or is not being done according to specifications. In that case I do not think the tax is exigible, and I take the risk of so advising. I think it ought to be laid down by the department that where the relationship of master and servant subsists, the tax is exigible. That would settle the question. It is a practical one in New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that would be
correct. Section 91, subsection 16, may have some bearing on the question. I am not sure whether the definition covers what the hon. gentleman has said, but it should be taken into account in deciding the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It would
have to be decided in the light of that definition, but on a hurried reading the definition does not seem to lessen the force of my suggestion that if there was not the right of dismissal but merely the right of cancellation he would not be an employee within the meaning of the act. It says, "Any salary, wage, remuneration, compensation," and so forth. Of course, consideration for a contract may be termed compensation-and yet it is not true compensation.

Subsection 5 of section 91 states that every employer at the time of payment of earnings to an employee shall deduct and collect the tax imposed, if the earnings are in excess of the stated amount. Does the employer have to make a return if the earnings are under that amount? If an employer knows, as a fact, that earnings are under the stated amount, must he make a return? For

Income War Tax Act

instance, would a man who has working for him, at his summer place, a person receiving only $600 a year, have to make a return?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The employer goes by the rate at the time. If the rate is such that if continued for twelve months the annual earnings would be above the minimum, then such employer must make the deduction. If not, the employer does not have to deduct.
He does not have to make any return?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Subsection 5 does not give the employer a reasonable number of days, namely the time between June 2 and July 1, to take care of his pay sheets. This national defence tax is one of the most iniquitous taxes possible. When the government imposes the heavy burden indicated under schedule A, and then tacks on this alditional burden, it is going beyond the powers it should exercise in respect of the small wage-earners. Large departmental stores and many other employers of labour will not, between now and July 1, have sufficient time to make out the schedules in conformity with the statute. The time is too short. I suggest it should be August 1.

When the resolution was before the committee I made inquiry with regard to regulations applying to farmers. My understanding was that a farmer was given the privilege of employing casual help for a definite period before he was required to make a return. According to subsection 6, if the daily rate is $3 a day the farmer would be required to send in a return, even if he had casual labour for only two days. Would the minister make some concession in this connection, so that a man would have to hire casual labour for a week or two weeks before being required to make a return? The actual incomes of many casual workers who receive $3 a day for stooking or threshing operations in western Canada would fall far below the figures set out in the act.
When the resolution was under discussion I raised the question as to the number of farmers across Canada who made returns last year. Many farmers had no idea that the act affected them, and consequently did not make returns. Has the minister any information as to the number of farmers across Canada who made returns last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I have no information available as to the number.

Would consideration be given to the extension of the period during

which casual labourers may work before the employer becomes liable for prosecution upon failing to make returns?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have in mind the circumstances of employment of a part-time gardener. He may tend half a dozen gardens. For instance, there is a man who puts in my garden and looks after it all summer. He goes and comes when he pleases, keeps his own time and puts in his bill at the end of the month. But he may be doing that work for six other people. I pay no attention to what he does when he leaves my place. I am not going to chase up and down to see whom the man is working for, and I have not done it. I have not felt guilty, nor do I believe I have defrauded the government of any revenue. But there ought to be some provision in the law with respect to that kind of employment. Any attempt to drive employers into making a return in circumstances of that kind is unworkable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Replying to the hon. member for Mackenzie, I do not believe we should make any change in the law. As it now stands, if a person is receiving wages at more than the minimum rate the deduction must be made. I do not know where we would start if we attempted to prescribe periods. At any rate that has not been done.
There is no difficulty in respect of most employees. They are on the big payrolls, where substantial numbers of men and women are employed. There are many of these odd cases which present extreme difficulties. As the leader of the opposition has said, in some instances employers will not pay much attention, because they realize the revenues would not amount to anything. In other cases they do amount to something, and I cannot take the position that the law should not be obeyed and observed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, but what action does the department take to learn whether or not there are evasions? Is it just one of those cases where a check cannot be made, and nothing is done? Does the department check the returns which come in, and leave it at that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Investigations are made at the place where the employee works.

I learned of two incidents lately which may be of interest to the minister. The owner of a property asked a carpenter what it would cost to erect a fence between his property and that of his neighbour, and was quoted a price of $24. Having submitted a price, I suppose the carpenter would be in the category of a contractor.

Income War Tax Act
The owner of the property in question felt it unnecessary to make any deduction. Another owner of property sent for a carpenter to repair his verandah. He did not ask for a price, but when the carpenter had finished the work he handed the owner a bill for $18. In that instance the owner must make provision for the tax. I am sure there must be countless thousands of cases where the government receives no revenue at all.

In all instances the deductions for national defence tax are made by corporations, business concerns and so on. In the event of the national defence tax being deducted by a corporation from the pay of an employee, and in the further event of its being ascertained at the end of the year that earnings sufficient to bring the employee under the tax have not been earned, who applies for the return of what has been paid? Is the responsibility with the employee or the employer?
I have in mind the fact that deductions are taken weekly from the pay of employees who might not come under the tax. Many employees are not familiar with the regulations- in fact many hon. members sitting in this chamber are not as familiar with them as they should be-and as a result many who would be entitled to a refund do not understand the procedure necessary to secure a refund. If an employer is making a deduction he should be compelled to keep records, and if deductions are made from the pay of an employee who, it is found, has not come under the act, such employer should be responsible for applications for refunds. Is it right to assume that the individual must make application for a return of funds collected, if he does not come under the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The employee is the one who makes application. If, however, he wishes to make arrangements with his employer to apply on his behalf, or on behalf of all the employees, well and good; in fact such an arrangement would add greatly to the convenience of the department.
That arrangement could be made with employees where they have an organization? An understanding could be arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have
no doubt that on a large number of contracts of employment no tax at all is paid. It must be so in the very nature of things. The honest employer will do everything the statute says, but the casual employer may not. The only 14873-2164
way to get this tax checked and collected is to pass a regulation requiring every man who hires out his services to carry a pass book, in which should be entered every dollar he earns, initialed by his employer and accessible to the government, so that the whole thing may be checked. Otherwise there will be evasions. There must be a better system than the present. It is all right in the case of permanent employers, big corporations with large payrolls and a large number of employees. They will do it in order to protect themselves, but in the smaller cases it will be ignored.

There must be a considerable number of people who do not have to pay the tax, their annual income not amounting to $660, or $1,200 in the case of married men, but who will not receive a refund of the money they have paid in. It would involve a great deal of bureaucracy, considerable bookkeeping, to keep track of every employee and employer. Would it not be more efficient to require persons who receive over $660 or $1,200 to make a return, as in the case of income tax? The employee might be asked to send in his returns and they could be checked over with the returns filed by those employing him. Has the minister anything to say with regard to such a system, whereby the whole procedure might be clarified and made more efficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The whole principle is
deduction at the source. In many cases returns will be made by these taxpayers, but in other cases the returns will not be made because the deductions will take place through the year. This provides a means of collecting the tax evenly over the year, and in any event it was felt, at the time the tax was introduced, that instead of waiting until the end of the year and then asking employees to make a return the deduction should be made throughout the period. I am sure a considerably larger proportion of the tax payable will be collected by the government under this method, because there will be quite a number who would spend it otherwise and to whom the payment of a lump sum at the end of the year would be extremely difficult, although they would not mind it so much if they had it deducted in this way.

I am thinking of the person who does not have to pay the tax directly but from whom it is deducted. Many of these people do not know that there is a refund coming to them for the reason that their income does not come up to the specified amount. I believe the change to $660 is from the 1st of January, 1941?
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is $660 from the 1st of July, 1941, not from the 1st of January.
Mr. O'BRIEN: I do not like to delay the committee but I wish to revert to the subject I was discussing a little while ago. I refer to the definition of piece worker or employee. I may have a quaint idea of my position in this house, but I believe I am here to help to make these laws that we are passing, in conjunction with 244 other members. If that is so, I do not know why the minister should tell me that I ought to consult a lawyer to find out the meaning of any law in the making of which I am supposed to be helping.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I said not to.
Mr. O'BRIEN: I asked for some information and the minister said: "This is a very mild legal question, but not one about which it would be necessary to consult a solicitor."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is right.
Mr. O'BRIEN: If it is a legal question and I do not need to consult a solicitor, then I shall have to go to a crystal gazer because I do not know where to get the information. In this house we are entitled to information. If members cannot obtain information we can readily understand the confusion that must exist in the country.
I believe the word "bureaucracy" has been used, and earlier in the day the minister said we should not allow the impression to leave this house that we are trying to establish anything of the sort. Perhaps not; but if on a simple question like this members of parliament cannot find out what the law means, a law which they are making, how in the world can people who are doing business in the country possibly expect to cope, not only with these techncial regulations but with the mass of information that is demanded by every department in the federal government and in the provinces? Why, one department wanted to know how much sawdust we were burning in our saw mill. Sawdust is a nuisance, and they said to use a 2,000-pound ton, just in case one might be using one of 2,240 pounds. That sort of information is voluminous, and yet in the maritime provinces, while there are several large companies, there are other concerns in the owner-managed category. There are hundreds of small companies whose business records can be carried in one's vest pocket, so that the information will not be obtained by the government until the officials in the department have some actual knowledge of what does happen from the time a man is hired until he gets his pay cheque and the goods that are produced are sold. An efficiency expert has been described 
as a man who knows more and more about less and less until he knows everything about nothing. It seems to me we are rapidly approaching that point in our economic life, and it is getting to the stage where all the discussion in this house seems to be concerned with the rich individual or the big corporation. But all this taxation, at any rate a great deal of it, is coming out of the owner-managed type of business, and unless that type of business is sustained and the government recognizes it as worth while in the- economic set-up, then it will vanish and the owner-managed type of business will eventually be a museum piece.
It is all very well for these regulations to be exacted from large corporations, because they can continue adding clerks to their organization until of course the business can no longer stand the strain. Then, as so often happens, these corporations go through the wringer-corporations never die. All the money that is put into them by the public is squeezed out. But the individual has to face his own responsibility; he cannot dodge the issue. If we are to go on employing people in this country with some degree of stability, that type of thing should be safeguarded, and that I am afraid is what we are beginning to call bureaucracy. I think the people are getting a little afraid of Ottawa and the regulations coming therefrom. I believe the provinces are afraid of Ottawa. Perhaps that is one reason why the Sirois commission report was not accepted. When we down in the mari-times have something happen within our own provincial jurisdiction under the British North America Act, we believe we are reasonably close to the government and the government is reasonably close to the people; but with a national issue in Ottawa that situation does not prevail. I believe that the people are of the opinion that a bureaucracy has been built up, and if the minister fears that opinion is going abroad in the land then he as a member of the government should see that more, shall I say, common sense business principles, are applied to the Department of Finance so that what I might call this pseudo-efficiency may vanish.

I was not present in the chamber this morning when the minister evidently cautioned hon. members in regard to the danger of giving the impression that bureaucracy was increasing in this country. Possibly the minister was wise in cautioning hon. members in that regard, because it is very easy to give the impression that there is bureaucracy in government. But we can have a bureaucracy that is not in government. And it is the people in Canada who insist on

Income War Tax Act
being bureaucratic in their business who object to bureaucracy in government. If we are to have bureaucracy in Canada I would certainly rather have a bureaucracy over which the people have some control than one over which the people have no control at all. It is merely a choice of which kind of bureaucracy we are going to have. We can have a managed bureaucracy in Canada or a bureaucracy imposed on the people by a plutocracy. That is what you are going to have. So that there is not much choice. I am all for the bureaucracy that we can control so far as it may be controlled through parliament. There are other things that could be said in connection with that.
I am not going to take up time suggesting that this defence tax be reduced. We have already done that. But there are certain considerations involved. First, there is the consideration that those who are liable to payment of the tax because of the wages or salaries that they receive should not evade payment. I do not know whether the minister is satisfied that he is getting all the tax that should be collected in that way or not. On the other hand there is the consideration that those who are not liable for the tax, because they do not receive a wage that brings them within the act, should not be compelled to pay and then those deductions not be returned to them. I think the minister stated last year that the intention was that tax payments made should not bring the wage or salary below the minimum figure. Take a person receiving a salary of almost $1,200, say $1,190. That person, if he were making out an income tax report to the department himself, would not pay any tax at all. But this tax is deducted at the source. Unless he makes application-and I imagine that the application has to be supported in some way that is satisfactory to the minister or the department -he will have paid approximately $60, a month's wage, which he should not pay and on which he will be unable to get a refund.
There is considerable merit in the proposal of the leader of the opposition that every employee should carry a book in which would be entered by his employer the amount of wages received and the amount of tax deducted. Then at the end of the year all that employee would have tj do would be to return his book to the Department of National Revenue and they could see what he had received in wages and whether there was any refund coming to him.
These, I insist, are important considerations, and some way should be found of working them out. We should be sure that those who are liable to the tax should pay their share, but those who are not liable because they do
not receive a wage which is sufficient to bring them under the tax, should not have to pay it, and if it is deducted from their wages a refund should be made.

The minister should give us something more definite. The suggestion made by the leader of the opposition is a pretty good one. I employ quite a variety of labour, some on my farm, some in town in the garden; I have a large block on which at times I have painting and decorating done, and taking off the storm windows generally takes a day or so. I should like to know why the minister could not have a book or something of the sort that could be entered up. In making my annual return there is not room on the forms for me to put in the number of labourers and what I pay and so on, so that I always send in a separate statement with respect to the labour I employ, the hours they work, wages paid and so forth. I want to make an honest return. As I see it I shall have to deduct from every one of these labourers a certain percentage. What would the minister do if he were in my position? I employ a painter for a few days, or a decorator, and I supply the material; or there is the labourer in the garden. What would the minister do if he were in my position, assuming the act to be as it is now?
