In regard to these refunds, does the employee have to set out how many days he worked, how much he received and how much was deducted, or could he make a blanket claim just pointing out that he did not receive sufficient to bring him under the act, and ask the department to return the money deducted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He has to make his claim on the prescribed form. He has to show how much he has earned, where, from whom and how much has been deducted.

I suppose it would not be possible for the department to do the bookkeeping for him if he put in a claim, knowing that he was under the minimum? It is obvious that most of these men cannot keep continuous records themselves. The government, on the other hand, will have the records of the employers, and I presume they must have a system under which they have an entry for each individual. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That might be possible if he worked the whole year for one employer.

Of course it would be very simple in that case, but if he had a number of jobs he would not know how many days he actually worked. Perhaps he just made enough to get along, and earned less than the minimum. Would not the government have the figures in regard to that

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

There have been no
prosecutions.

I imagine there are
in Canada employers who have made the deductions but have failed to report them, though I do not know of any myself. What machinery has the government to check up on whether or not all the money collected from employees is finding its way to the treasury? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The income tax inspectors in the various districts would have a pretty good idea whether any employers were holding back. If the inspectors were not getting returns from people whom they knew to be in business, presumably they would look into that. I have no reason for thinking that any employers at all have made the deductions and put the money into their own pockets. That would be theft, a criminal offence and a very serious offence under present conditions. I think if they deduct the money they remit it. There may be cases of delay; I do not know about that.

In supplementary form T4, which has to be filed by an employer, will it be necessary for the employer to give the name of every person to whom he pays wages at the rate of over $600 a year and from whom he deducts the national defence tax? I know that must be done in connection with those more or less permanently employed, but what about temporary employees who work for only a day or two?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Those names have to be filed also, because if an application for refund is made we have to refer to the employers' returns in order to find out whether the tax has been deducted.

Will there be a limit on the time within which these refunds will be made? Will that be six months after the end of the year, or what? I should think you would require a limit; otherwise you would not be able to balance your books very well.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The application for refund has to be filed within one year. That is the time limit.
And what is the time limit within which the employer must make his return to the government?

Mr. O'NEILL: It has been said repeatedly that many people who are paid at more than the minimum rate required before this taxation is imposed, do not work enough during the year to become liable to the tax, but the employers have collected that tax from month to month. On section 29-Machinery or equipment.

It seems to me there is serious objection to the possible retroactive effect of this section. Section 90 as originally enacted in 1939 provided that certain deductions might be made in connection with moneys expended prior to April 30 for work actually

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act by empowering the minister, subject to the advice and representations of the advisory committees, to undertake certain minor rehabilitation projects and schemes and enter into agreements with respect thereto, provided that if the total amount to be expended under any such single project or scheme exceeds five

thousand dollars in any fiscal year the approval of the governor in council shall be required; also to authorize the minister to pay administrative expenses and travelling and living expenses of officials and employees.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister make his statement at this stage, or would he prefer to make it after we go into committee?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I prefer to do it in the committee stage.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Vien in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, under the bill as now drafted provision is made under section 12, for example, for the purchase of machinery by the minister up to an amount of $5,000, and there is provision for selling machinery not to exceed $500. Section 10 as it is now in the bill is the section under which provision is made for entering into agreements with provinces, municipalities and persons for doing certain things, such as taking over of lands which are to be placed in community pastures, or to be irrigated, or to be taken out of cultivation and perhaps seeded down to grass. But other works are undertaken such as the building of small dams, which probably cost $175, and small dug-outs on farms, which probably cost from $50 to $100. These have always been passed by the minister since the act was first set up. Other acts do make provision that expenditures up to $5,000 can be made by the minister and that anything over $5,000 requires an order in council. That is true, for example, with respect to public works.
It has been assumed ever since this act was passed in 1935 that expenditures up to $5,000 could properly be made under the general practice in the departments, but the auditor general questions the possibility of continuing the practice without special provision being made therefor in the legislation. It is therefore proposed that the act be amended by repealing section 10 and making it possible for the minister to pass upon these smaller projects. As it now stands, minor schemes and undertakings of the kind could not, according to the opinion given by the auditor general, properly be dealt with without the approval of council, and it is thought to be inadvisable that the smaller projects should be taken to council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Was there a legal opinion as to the legality of the former practice, or is it that the auditor general of his own motion has questioned the procedure?

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not think a legal opinion has been asked for or given, unless it was obtained through the auditor general's branch, but last summer they were disputing the right of payment under the legislation as it now stands. Up until that time, speaking from memory, I do not think they had disputed it at all.

There is one thing I do not understand about this legislation. In the first place the idea of it was to help farmers who were suffering from the drought and did not expect a harvest or who had suffered from poor crops in previous years. The purpose of the legislation was, of course, to increase production, to permit those who had had a succession of bad crops to harvest more wheat. But since then there has been a great change. There has been the policy of the curtailment of the production of wheat, and some farmers are to be paid now not to grow wheat. But here in this legislation we are starting out again to give to those who have been unable to get very much wheat from their lands the opportunity to produce more wheat. It seems contradictory from beginning to end. I am strongly opposed to it. I think it is absurd. In the first place you say: cultivate more; in the second place, cultivate less; in the third place, cultivate more and cultivate lessl I do not understand it at all.
If we had such legislation in the province of Quebec all the prairie members would be on their feet protesting against it. But we cannot get anything from the Department of Agriculture for the province of Quebec. I remember the time when the older provinces could get anything because they were able to say they were not bankrupt. But in the west the farmer said to the municipality that he was bankrupt. Then the municipality said to the province that the municipality was bankrupt. Then the province said to Ottawa that the province was bankrupt. And then everything was given to them and we had to empty our pockets for them. A queer idea, surely, of preaching unity in this country. I cannot understand it. And now they are coming here again with this legislation. I am opposed to it. I find it nonsensical.
I remember the time, Mr. Chairman, when Mr. Dunning and Mr. Rogers were on the stand and I asked them if the western provinces had paid their interest. I remember I was told that Manitoba was doing fairly well, and Alberta was doing fairly well, but Saskatchewan had not paid its interest or very little. Mr. Dunning admitted that, and Mr. Rogers admitted it. The other provinces now
have less revenue. Hon. members will remember my stand on the succession duties act, and here we are being asked to pay more to encourage this sort of thing. If it is sensible to pay farmers not to produce grain, how can we, on the other hand, spend money to give them the opportunity to produce more grain?
I would like to have an answer to satisfy my mind.

Perhaps the minister is
not going to answer at the moment. I would judge from the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata that the minister is not depending on him to get this amendment through.
I am not the only one who thinks like that.

The minister referred to
the fact that this legislation came into force in 1935. At that time an advisory committee was set up and for a year or two it played an important part in the work which was done in that regard. This rehabilitation legislation, under the minister, has on the whole served a useful purpose in the west in the matter of conservation of water, the seeding of certain areas to grass, and the establishment of community pastures. But I have a grievance in relation to the way in which the act has been administered-I was going to say particularly as regards the machinery set up to administer the act in the last two years. I should like the minister to state to what extent this advisory committee has made representations to the minister, say, in the last year, and to what extent its recommendations have been accepted and acted upon.
The minister indicated that under this amendment he proposes to proceed with certain small projects, and among others he mentioned dams. I would ask him to give the committee some indication as to the number of projects he has in mind. Does he propose to go ahead with the scheme outlined last year in respect of dams, and in connection with which some preparatory work was done by way of the surveying of ravines leading into the Qu'Appelle river? Several sites were surveyed and set out at which dams would be constructed, and it was the intention, I believe, to proceed in the very near future. Does the minister propose to go ahead with that work?-because I might say here and now that I am not very much in favour of the scheme. We should have a definite statement from the minister.
I have a grievance in respect of the work carried on last year, more particularly in connection with dug-outs, and I shall state



Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
the grievance now. The dug-out scheme was inaugurated to give relief to farmers so that they could help themselves. The farmers made application to the proper authorities and received approval of their schemes, and they were supposed to do the work themselves, receiving about $150 for their labour. It was purely a relief measure. The idea was to give the farmer $150 to do the work, helping him by placing in his possession that amount of money, and also providing a water supply for his operations. There has been started what I consider to be a real racket with respect to the installation of these dug-outs. Certain contractors who had the machinery to do the work-the drag lines and ditch machinery-proceeded to make agreements with different farmers to do the work for them, and to collect the $150 in each instance from the department. This procedure was approved by the department. The contractors were in a position to put in hundreds of these dug-outs-a great many more than would otherwise have been possible.
I was invited to attend a certain meeting at which one of these contractors was to appear. I did not attend, may I say, but I learned after the meeting that the contractor had signed up many of the farmers for the installation of dug-outs on their farms. The contractor had the farmer sign an agreement in which it was stated that the contractor would do the work and receive power of attorney from the farmer to collect the money. My grievance is that while the face of the agreement bears the signature of a witness to the farmer's signature, no witness was present. I have in my hand one of the agreements purporting to have been signed by a witness. That witness was not at the meeting, and did not see the farmer sign. In fact the farmer who signed did not really know that this was the form he had signed. I have also a copy of a power of attorney taken from the farmer by the contractor. This too is signed by the witness, who was not present at the time the power of attorney was given.
I went to the contractor and asked him for the copy of the agreement I have in my hand. He gave it to me. I asked him for the power of attorney, and he gave me that also. When he opened his briefcase I saw that he had at least fifty of these documents already signed by the witness-and I have his name here. Those documents were all ready to be used wherever he went to secure a farmer's signature. The signatures, therefore were not witnessed at all.
There is one further point with respect to dug-outs. A number of farmers contracted for two, and some for three. A contractor who was building a dug-out on a man's farm

suggested to the farmer, "Why not put in another one, while I have the machinery here?" The farmer replied, "Well, that would be all right with me, if I could do it." "Well," said the contractor, "the inspector will be here to-day. We will have him approve your application, and in that way I can do the job while I am here, and it will not be necessary to come back to do the work later." The inspector came and the application was made up. When it became necessary to have a witness to the second agreement he had made, and to the power of attorney the contractor was taking for the construction of the second dug-out, the question was asked, "How about a witness?" The inspector replied, "Well, your wife may witness this." When the farmer's wife took the pen to affix her signature the inspector said, "Just a minute, Mrs. So-and-So, you had better sign your maiden name; it would look better in the department, and it would be easier to have it approved."
I know of other cases of the kind-and all this happens in connection with the spending of public money. The farmer about whom I have been speaking did not want a second dug-out; he did not want even the first one. But he had attended a meeting where all the farmers were signing agreements for dug-outs, and he said, "Well, I will get in the swim."
I do not believe that was the intention, even of the minister. I appeal to him to see that that sort of thing is stopped. I am not accusing the minister, nor am I suggesting that he knows what was going on. But I have evidence before me showing that agreements were witnessed before they were signed. I do not believe the minister is the kind of man who wrould like to have that going on. I have brought the facts to his attention.
As I have said on other occasions, much useful work has been done under this act. At the present time however I believe there is a limit to which the development can be carried. The act has served its purpose. I do not believe there is much necessity for further developments. I suggest the minister ought not to proceed this summer with a general programme involving the building of large numbers of dams, as I understand is the intention in respect of the tributaries of and the ravines leading into the Qu'Appelle river.
I would ask the minister to make a statement respecting these matters. I appeal to him to have these practices stopped to which I especially referred.

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Perhaps I should deal first with the observations of the hon. member for Temiscouata. He suggests that these dams were built for the purpose of assisting in graingrowing operations. That of course was not the intention. The intention in 1935 when the procedure was first adopted, under a previous government, was the very opposite. I believe it was the intention to provide water for live stock in some sections which are comparatively dry. The water is put into small dams and dug-outs for the purpose of encouraging the raising of live stock on farms which previously had been largely given over to grain growing.
At that time there was some question, and there is still some question, as to whether grain farms on their past basis should be continued. At the same time it was provided that some of these lands should be re-grassed, or that some system should be followed which would embrace the possibility of stopping soil drift by sowing rye grass, or something of the kind, thereby taking it out of cultivation. That part of the work is still going on. It is apparent therefore that the objective behind the construction of dug-outs and building of small dams was not that of growing more grain. So far as I am aware, a number of dams have been built for the purpose of encouraging irrigation. That irrigation is on a small scale, when compared with the irrigation projects in the larger areas of Alberta. Again however the intention was to make it possible for people to get away from grain growing and to operate their farms in conjunction with pasture lands suitable for live stock rather than depending upon grain growing for their livelihood. I make these observations only to indicate that the intention was not that of producing more wheat, any more than is the present policy one of producing more wheat.
I agree with the last remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. If what he has described as having taken place in one or two instances has, in fact, taken place, then of course I should like to be provided with definite information. I should like to have the names of the persons concerned, including the name of the inspector who took the action indicated: because it is not the intention of any officials in the department or of myself that business should be conducted in that way.
When the hon. member states that the installation of dug-outs "last year" became a racket, I believe he was referring to 1939 rather than 1940. A practice had been growing up of making applications for dug-outs 14873-2171
in much greater numbers than could properly be installed in any one year. That was true right from 1935 on. In 1935, possibly four or five times as many applications were made as there were dug-outs constructed or even started; those applications were carried on into the succeeding year, and even in 1936 the number of dug-outs constructed was comparatively small. At that time the amount which was allowed in payment for moving earth was three cents a cubic yard. As most members know, earth cannot be moved at three cents a cubic yard with any kind of equipment. It was, however, intended that this would pay possibly a third of the cost of the dug-out. The farmer would take his own team and do the excavating, and this cash would provide him, while he was constructing the dug-out, with something to pay for a pump and any other necessities which he might have to buy for cash. It was not intended at the beginning that this payment should be so much a relief matter, because three cents a cubic yard could not have given him any considerable amount of relief.
In 1936, or 1937-1 am speaking from memory-the three cents a cubic yard was increased to four and a half cents, the idea being that the farmers at that time had to buy their feed and were not able to construct dug-outs unless they purchased grain, and they thought they needed more money with which to make a start. For two years the scheme was operated on a basis of four and a half cents a cubic yard. During that time comparatively few dug-outs were constructed.
In southern Manitoba there had developed a practice under which the municipalities secured drag-lines and excavated these dug-outs for the farmers in the community. Provision was made by the municipality for taking care of the amount which had to be paid over and above what was paid to each farmer. The money was paid to the municipality, and it was finally agreed, that we would accept the assignments made by the farmers to the municipal council for the amount that was payable to them. That developed into the plan which has been referred to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
On every occasion when any change was made in policy it was submitted to this advisory committee that has been mentioned, and they argued for these particular changes ini amounts and in, the different methods of undertaking the construction. The strongest argument that prevailed was to the effect that during the drought period, when farmers were unable to provide even hay or grain, it was impossible to have horses in condition to go to the bottom of a thirteen-foot hole and bring
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

earth up. They did make provision at first to dig the first four and a half feet by means of horses and to complete the last six or seven feet in the bottom with draglines, the horses taking off the top four and a half feet in the first twenty-four hours and the draglines coming and cleaning up the job. They were digging about one a day.
Variations of the -methods were submitted to the committee. In 1938, I believe it was, the amount was raised to six cents a cubic yard, again on the advice of the committee, the idea being that they were not able at that time to get farmers, on account of lack of crops and so forth, to construct dug-outs, and they wanted the dug-outs there when they got moisture. We consented to six cents. I must admit that during the time the scheme was operated on the basis of six cents there did develop some conditions that could not be adhered to for any great length of time. I attended the meeting of the committee in the spring of 1939 and objected to the six-cent rate for dugouts constructed by dragline, and I had to argue against most of the committee. I finally stated that I would reduce the rate to four and a half cents that fall whether -they liked it or not, and- it was finally reduced.
During 1939 there were a great many dug-outs constructed on the -basis of the six-cent rate, and, as hon. members know, the amount of money which was voted by this house for the purpose was exceeded. That is, there was an accumulation of applications over the whole previous three or four years during which the plan had been in operation. No method had been set up that would prevent farmers from going ahead and digging those which had been authorized in previous years; and on the accumulation, and with the operation of the drag-lines just prior to the outbreak of the war, when contractors had very little to do and used their draglines for this purpose, many more dug-outs were constructed than anyone had anticipiated in any one year, with the result that these payments had to be made last year.
I can understand why some of my friends have said-they have said it on previous occasions-that there were certain reasons for that; but I would recall once more that in the spring of 1939, in the month of May I believe-the records are all there-this whole matter was discussed in the advisory committee. I think every member of the committee will agree that it was the minister who argued for a reduction to four and a half cents and insisted upon it. As a matter of fact, in the fall of 1939 I personally stopped the further construction of dug-outs because they had exceeded the expenditure, and hon.

members, partcularly those from the west, will remember that there was a great deal of criticism all through the fall of 1939, through the winter of 1939-40 and well into the summer of 1940 as a result of the action which was then taken. With the payments finally cleared up, the regulations under which we are operating now, the instructions under which the organization is carrying on, will not permit of their going beyond the amount of money actually voted. Therefore this year we are operating on the four and a half-cent rate per cubic yard, and operating under conditions where the amount of money voted will not be exceeded.
In referring to the matter of the Qu'Appelle valley, I can only say that engineering groups have been investigating the possibilities of irrigation development both north and south of Qu'Appelle valley and the streams running into Qu'Appelle, and in the Qu'Appelle valley itself. The information is not sufficiently complete at present to enable one to say whether the plan will be proceeded with or otherwise. My view at the moment would be probably the amount of irrigation which can be carried on in these areas will be quite limited, largely on account of the amount of water which will be available for irrigation purposes. There are other works which were put in many years ago, back about 1904, or somewhere about that time, on the Qu'Appelle west, in the vicinity of Long lake. Some of these are giving some difficulty now, as I am sure the hon. member for Lake Centre will agree. They are causing difficulty in connection with the level of the water in Long lake. There is some discussion going on with the committee concerned with summer resorts above Long lake regarding that, but until we have a complete report from the engineers with regard to the whole matter, I would not be prepared to say what will be done in connection with this development.

I always listen with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Temiscouata. This afternoon, however, I could not accept the views he expressed. I have not visited the hon. member's constituency, but from what I have seen of the beautiful province of Quebec, the probability of shortage of water would not be very real in many areas of that province.
In Saskatchewan and the prairies, however, large areas have been settled with a view to engaging in extensive wheat farming. Those areas were settled when it was taken for granted that there would be a sufficient supply of moisture to ensure a profitable industry. Through no fault of the farmers many of those areas have not received sufficient moisture.

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
The work carried on under this legislation has meant a great deal to many people, and therefore I hope the hon. member for Temis-couata will not object too seriously to the carrying on of this important work.
What I rose to say was to express thanks to the minister for extending the work into northeastern Saskatchewan. Many hon. members have suggested that mixed farming might be developed much more extensively in western Canada. But where people have to haul water three or four miles, the raising of live stock presents a real problem. Through the work carried on under this administration, a great many farmers have been able to construct dug-outs and have adequate water for the entire year, and the money appropriated has been money very well spent.
In my constituency there has been some discussion in connection with the providing of a dam on the Assiniboine river north of Preeceville. I understand that this dam, if completed, would benefit the town of Kam-sack to a considerable extent. Would the minister give some indication whether the policy is to provide dams of that sort? I understand that the money required would be sufficient to construct a great many dug-outs for individual farmers. If there were plenty of money available to carry on both types of work, there might be some argument for putting in the larger dams, but in the meantime I think all the money available should be used to provide dams for individual farmers so that they might be self-supporting to a greater extent than they have been. Would the minister make some statement in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I shall be in a much better position to discuss the financial features of the programme when my estimates are before the committee, whether to-night or at some later time. I have not the books before me at the moment. I believe the estimates will be before the committee to-night, and I could discuss these items better at that time if hon. members will permit.

I take the opportunity to say through the Chair to my friend the hon. member for Mackenzie, who is very popular in this house and whose speeches are always appreciated by every hon. member, that he does not understand my point of view at all. I hope that situation will be changed in a few minutes.
In the first place, my constituency is one in which are to be found mixed farming, settlers and so forth. They are people who are accustomed to live by themselves, and they ask nothing unless they see people in
the same circumstances in other parts of the country receiving something. Then they say, "How is it that those people get so much and we in this part of the country do not?" It is just as if they had smallpox or diphtheria or some "other contagious disease and were put in quarantine. Nobody complained so long as they were accorded the same opportunities as our friends in the west received, but when some farmers in the west are given privileges and the east is discriminated against, then the complaints start. My hon. friend will understand why that is so.
I do not discuss the usefulness of this programme. I am not in a position to do so because I am not an agricultural expert. If I were I would be in a better position than the hon. member or any agricultural representative of the west who is an expert, because I would not be biased and would not have to rely on the votes of the people concerned to form my opinion. Now, however, I am not biased when I speak of my people because they get nothing. I make the statement that they get nothing. I make the further statement that the Department of Agriculture as now constituted is not a dominion department; it is a prairie department, and the eastern, provinces cannot get anything out of it. That is the reason why I suggest the abolition of the dominion Department of Agriculture, and that the cost of it be distributed in proportion to the rural population of each province, so that everyone will be on the same footing. What good does it do the eastern farmer to be always reading in the papers that the western fanner gets a little more, a little more to-day and a little more to-morrow; that the day after to-morrow there will be something for him, and that next week he will have something more, a nice little toy to play with, while the other gets nothing in his stocking? The western farmer has always something new, a life-saver, good for the throat, a little dessert, and the other gets nothing. I find it unfair.

How about the cheese
bonus?
And the more the western farmer gets the more he complains.
What about apples?
What about the growing of fibre flax?

If everything that is given to the east is summed up and compared with everything that has been given to the west, no one will see through what was given to the
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

west. I mean by that that the west has received so much that it is impossible to see through what has been given.

What about the
St. Lawrence waterway?	.

That will not give five
cents to the eastern farmer.
Will it give anything to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. At the end of each session it has been customary to allow great leeway to hon. members, but a line must be drawn somewhere. The resolution before the committee purports to enable the minister to deal with small projects not exceeding $5,000 without the formality of an order in council, and provides for the necessity of an order in council for such projects as exceed $5,000. We shall not make much headway or observe the rules by comparing the amounts appropriated for the western provinces with those for the eastern provinces. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the resolution that is before them.

Yes, sir. I will now
describe it as I visualize it. There is a little stream, and a little dam will be built. It cannot be a big dam, but it will be left to the discretion of the minister. And there is some sand. But the little dam will be built, and then there will be a little pond. The little pond will help to fertilize a little ground on both sides of the little stream. Then part of that water will be used for mixed farming; but since hogs are fed grain, the remainder of the water will be used for the production of grain. Therefore it is only because some pasture is required for the hogs, and the hogs will produce bacon for the allies, that this can be called a war project.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members laugh, but this is the only possible explanation for calling the scheme a war project. I am sorry, but that is the only way I can see it as having anything to do with patriotism or serving the cause of the allies.

I should like to read the pertinent part of this resolution before commenting upon it:
. . . that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act by empowering the minister, subject to the advice and representations of the advisory committees, to undertake certain minor rehabilitation projects and schemes and enter into agreements with respect thereto, provided that if the total amount to be expended under any such single project or scheme exceeds five

thousand dollars in any fiscal year the approval of the governor in council shall be required; also to authorize the minister to pay administrative expenses and travelling and living expenses of officials and employees.
I am not arguing against the principle of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, or against the necessity for the expenditures that have 'been made under that act, or against the benefits that have accrued to the people of western Canada, giving them an opportunity to rehabilitate themselves. But, Mr. Chairman, if I may use the expression, I am inclined to be slightly suspicious as to the reasons that actuate the minister in introducing this amendment which on its face appears to be so innocuous. In the estimates for the current year, 1941-42, an amount of $2,500,000 is provided to be expended in connection with projects under that act. The system in vogue under the statute is for the minister to appoint an advisory committee, which advises the minister. As the minister admitted- although he said some of us were rather suspicious of the coincidence that it was the year before an election-in 1939 there were overexpenditures. That situation was dealt with in the auditor general's report, to which the minister made reference, and I should like to quote that report in reference to this matter. At page 61 I find the following:
Commitments of approximately $1,315,575.20 were incurred in excess of the amount appropriated without certificates of the comptroller of the treasury being secured in the manner provided for by sections 26 and 29 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931. These overcommitments, by group classifications, are made up of: land utilization, $22,036.47; water development, small projects, $909,553, large projects, $384,185.73.
I pause here to point out that under the statute authority was provided for the minister to make certain expenditures; yet in 1939 he exceeded the amount he was permitted to expend by over $1,300,000. Then the auditor general's report goes on to say:
By an amendment to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act .	.	. the minister may,
subject to the approval of the governor in council, enter into agreements with provinces, cities, towns, persons, etc., for projects or schemes for the conservation of water. Payments during the year were made in several cases on ministerial authority only, examples being payments to W. B. Ramsay, Regina, for construction in connection with the Magrath irrigation canal, $1,858.12 and to W. Y. McKinnon, Saskatoon, re the Castle river test hole, $2,755.58. Similarly, payments for stockwatering dams and community projects where the total cost did not exceed $5,000 were paid without the approval of the governor in council.
In consequence of the auditor general having drawn to the attention of this house and the country the overexpenditure made by the minister on his own authority, there was

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
a considerable amount of criticism. The minister now asks the house to amend the act as it now stands, and the amendment means this. Take a year when the minister might consider it necessary or advisable to overexpend the amount voted by this parliament and, in addition, to pay those who do the work, without the authority of this parliament. Apparently that is the reason for the introduction of this amendment. What does that mean? It means that parliament is asked to give the Minister of Agriculture the power, apart from any control by parliament, to expend any amount he chooses for such schemes as in his discretion he deems necessary, provided that the expenditure on any one project is less than $5,000 in any fiscal year.

And subject to the
advice and representations of the advisory committees.

Yes, subject to the advice of the advisory committee which-I make no criticism in this connection-no doubt is appointed upon the recommendation of the minister himself. In this connection I noticed that when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked' the minister whether he was bound by the representations of these committees, or whether he followed those representations in all instances, the minister made no reply. Therefore the stituation as it now stands, is that if parliament gives the minister the power he seeks in this amendment, he can expend any sum of money he may choose; he can spend that money where he chooses and when he chooses without any control on the part of this parliament over that expenditure, provided that in no single project is an amount of over $5,000 expended. If he wishes to develop larger projects and expend greater sums of money, he does not require the consent of this parliament, the consent of the representatives of the people, all he needs is the authority of an order in council.
I listened with interest to his explanation of the purposes of and the reasons behind this legislation, and I again make the protest which I have raised before with regard to other similar legislation, that parliament has a duty, and that duty is to control the expenditure of money. Expenditures should not be made without the authorization of parliament. In war time it is necessary that the .executive should have wide powers, but that does not justify this amendment. There has been a trend within this parliament in the last year to abdicate our rights to the governor in council to an ever increasing degree. The excuse may be given that we are at war.
This would apply to war measures, but it does not excuse the minister being given carte blanche to expend money as he sees fit on domestic matters not related to the war.
Those who now sit on the government benches were loud in their criticism of the former government of Mr. Bennett for passing orders in council, but there has been no greater offender in the history of Canada than the present government. Fourteen thousand orders in council have been passed since the outbreak of war, 4,908 since the present session of parliament began, 2,898 of which were passed while parliament was actually in session. Statutes have been amended and suspended in their operation, and in one instance access to the king's courts has been denied. This resolution is a continuation of the trend against which I protested at the time the minister introduced the summer-fallow vote.
In connection with non-war measures this parliament is being asked to place in the hands of the minister power to expend money without the control of parliament, subject only to the whim of the minister. I protest against this tendency. I approve the principle of the act, but I do not see why this committee should be asked to approve a course of conduct which has been condemned by the auditor general and which is contrary to the principles of representative government. We should not be asked to place in the hands of any one man, however estimable he may be, power to expend money without the necessity of authorization by parliament.
What is the programme for this year with regard to the construction of small dams and dug-outs?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not think the hon member was in the chamber a few moments ago when I replied to the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). I expect that my estimates will be up to-night, and a better opportunity will be accorded to discuss these matters. As a matter of fact, the Chairman has ruled that we are discussing the possibility of making payments up to $5,000, rather than questions of reconstruction and other matters like that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The principle contended for by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is an important one, and so far I have heard no defence of its breach by the minister. My recollection is that because of the drought conditions that existed in 1934 and 1935, the technical officers of the government suggested this form of rehabilitation and amelioration in certain parts of Canada. Notwithstanding what the hon.
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has said, I think there is a good deal of merit in this measure. I object, however, to this resolution having the appearance of a blank cheque, within certain limitations, in connection with new enterprises. There is no knowing to what extent the government may be committed under the principle of this resolution as it now stands. We should know exactly what is contemplated and what burden is to be placed upon the country.
By no stretch of the imagination can it be said that this. is a war measure. It is simply a continuation of a rehabilitation measure which was approved by parliament in days gone by. Experience has shown that this whole thing has run away with itself in so far as overexpenditures are concerned. There has been no real check on that aspect of the matter, which has called forth remonstrances from the auditor general. In 1931 we passed the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, the intention of which was clear. The intention was not only to discourage but absolutely to prohibit overexpenditure by departments in any field of enterprise that they might undertake. So far as I can see, the minister has taken to himself powers which at least the audit department does not consider he ought to possess. I am aware that there has been a different interpretation in connection with the matter, and this should be clarified by an opinion from the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I was not certain that there had been an option, but it has been sent to me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the minister read that before he finishes? I had an idea that an opinion had been given, but I was not quite certain as to the legal position and power of the minister, according to existing legislation. According to the wording of the legislation, there is no limitation upon the gross amount that may be expended by the minister; that is left to him to decide, provided that the expenditure does not go beyond $5,000 on any one project. Of course that is a negation of parliamentary government. If the minister had been here in 1931 and 1932, I have no doubt he would have joined in the chorus of condemnation against the theory of giving blank cheques to the government. I am looking at the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) at the moment, and he is shaking with laughter because he appreciates the allusion I am making. If the theory was bad then it is bad now, and it may be worse now because the country is at war and we should [Mr. R. B. Hanson.J
be more careful about these peace-time expenditures. As a matter of fact, I do not think the minister has made out a case for continuing these expenditures at the present time. I say that with great deference because I have not personal information. Of one thing, however, I am certain, namely, that the way this resolution is worded it is absolutely bad in principle, and the minister should not ask us to pass the resolution in its present terms.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
What is really being asked for appears in the bill itself which will be brought down later, and which conforms with the principle in many other acts and has been the principle adopted in connection with public works, I think, since confederation. I shall, however, deal with that in a moment.
For the time being I wish to refer to the fact already mentioned by others, that the first act dealing with this matter was passed in the spring of 1935. The date of the act is April 17, 1935. It is a very short act covering two sides of one sheet, and provides, first, for an advisory committee. It states, not the persons who are to constitute that committee, but the organizations whose officials shall constitute the committee. Then it goes on to provide that the committee shall consider and advise the minister as to the best methods to be adopted, in much the same terms as are used in the act with regard to the advisory committees that are there now. Then it provides:
No member of the committee shall receive any payment or emolument for his services.
Another section provides:
The minister may appoint such temporary technical, professional and other officers and employees as he may deem necessary and expedient for carrying out the provisions of this act and the salaries and expenses of such officers shall be fixed by the governor in council.
That is exactly the same section as is contained in the present act.
Another section provides:
The governor in council may make such regulations as may be necessary or expedient for the effectual execution and working of this act and the attainment of the intention and objects thereof.
That is, everything that was provided for in that act is contained in those few sections. The advisory committee is there which advises the government; and, as was said by the hon. member for Lake Centre, the principle has been in the act from the beginning, that the minister or those administering the act may take the advice of the committee. That is the meaning of "advisory". They may proceed otherwise or just as they choose after having had the benefit of the advice of the committee. To an extent, that is true and

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
has been true all the way through. Before we came into office-I am speaking from memory-there was only one meeting of that committee, and that was held very early in the setting up of the organization. There has been quite a number of meetings of the committee since.
The act of 1935 limited the amount of money that was to be expended. It provided:
For the purposes of this act the sum of seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars shall be appropriated and paid out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada during the fiscal year 1935-36 and for each fiscal year for a further period of four years a sum not exceeding one million dollars per annum as may be necessary to continue and extend the work undertaken under this act.
Then section 9 provides:
The minister shall annually lay before parliament a report of all proceedings under this act for the preceding fiscal year.
That is the whole act, and1 I would point out that unlimited authority is given there under order in council and within the amount of money which was voted by parliament, which in the first year was $750,000 and in each succeeding year, $1,000,000. In the first year the present government was in office the act was amended to remove the limitation on the amount and to make it the amount which was voted by parliament. From that year down to the present, only in one year has that amount been exceeded, namely, in 1939, and for the reasons I gave to the committee earlier in the discussion. I am sorry that the hon. member for Lake Centre was not in the chamber when I first explained the matter. I referred to the fact that this provision with respect to amounts under $5,000 is in the Public Works Act and that the same principle is followed by every department of the government in expenditures on public works.
The hon. member for Lake Centre quoted from the auditor general's report. I will again quote the same passage showing what the auditor general had to say:
Commitments of approximately $1,315,575.20 were incurred in excess of the amount appropriated without certificates of the comptroller of the treasury being secured in the manner provided for	by sections 26	and 29	of	the
Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931. These overcommitments, by group classifications, are made up of: land utilization, $22,036.47; water development, small projects, $909,553, large projects, $384,185.73.
The first thing I wish to say with regard to that is to reply to the suggestion made by the hon.	member	for Lake Centre	thatthis was an	election	year.	It was	not ofnecessity an	election	year,	and I	do	not
know that anyone had any idea that it was
going to be an election year. Furthermore, it did not turn out to be an election year. I do not think anyone had any idea, until within perhaps forty-eight hours of the time the election was declared, that there was going to be an election even in the year in which it was held. I suppose my statement to that effect will be used against me after I make my next statement. It is this, that if I paid half as much attention to politics as my hon. friends think I do and had been half as much the politician as some of them think I am I would not in September and October, 1939, have stopped expenditures upon small dug-outs, dams and structures of every kind in connection with these water undertakings, simply because, under the programme as it was then being carried on, these works were exceeding the expenditures. It is true that some works could not be cut off immediately. If they had all been cut off immediately, it is true that there would have been an overexpenditure when I discovered it in September and October when I was in western Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It was
the minister's duty to cut them off.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
And he did cut them
off, but there was an overexpenditure for the reasons I have stated, and some of the criticisms which have been made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle are justified by the facts as they then existed. If they had not been justified, the expenditures would probably not have been) stopped in the manner in which they were. But they were stopped' and stopped within three or four months of the time the election was called.
Again I repeat what every member from western Canada knows, that I, in common with every member who contested a constituency on behalf of the government of Canada, had to meet criticisms to the effect not only that these expenditures were cut off but that the farmers were told and contractors were told that they could not receive payment even for works which had been done until the whole matter had been placed before the House of Commons and the money voted in order to meet the payments.

Did the minister not
allow contractors to continue to take new contracts knowing that they were not going to get the money for another year?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I do not know of any contracts that were let on that basis, but I know that some contractors said that they were going to go on and complete their contracts, believing that the government of Canada, whatever government was in power
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

and whether or not an election was held, would recognize the liability of the government to pay for those contracts. Tenders had been properly called for and contracts let; under these circumstances some contractors said that they were prepared to proceed and complete their contracts, and they did.
I told one contractor that he was taking chances and he said, "I am willing to take chances".

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think it has been the general practice of governments to permit contractors to take those chances. As a matter of fact, it has been the custom here, ever since I have been in the house, and I think it has been the custom since confederation, that moneys are voted for public works, contracts are let, and certain moneys are expended in one year while certain moneys are spent in another year. When money is not sufficient, then further money is voted in supplementary estimates in another year in order to take care of the work. The contractor goes on with the operations, and the money as finally voted is paid. That has been done, and I believe it has been the general practice. The dredging of the St. Lawrence river is in exactly the same classification. Many other works in connection with which that practice is followed could be mentioned to the committee.
In any event, however, there was an overexpenditure of money; I admit there was a much larger overexpenditure of money than should be allowed under any act of this kind. Immediately I found there was to be an overexpenditure, I put a stop to it, and cancelled the authorization. I cancelled any contracts which could be cancelled at that time.
What control is there on the part of the minister to ascertain at any time how much has been expended? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The control that exists in connection with all works of this kind, whether provincial or federal, is the control of the amount of money voted for'a particular purpose. The amount of money voted in this particular instance was $2,500,000. That will appear in the estimates, as they will be brought before the committee-probably to-night. That is the limitation as to the amount of money which may be expended.
The limitation in the department, under the present provision, is that we divide that money, and we say, "We intend to spend so much on dug-outs, so much on small dams, so much on large projects, so much on grass, and so much on other things." The comptroller has insisted that this be done, and we

have done it. If we do want to make an expenditure in one line in excess of what we had intended in the beginning, we can make it only if we have not expended all our money in some other section, and we have the expenditure of that money authorized by transferring it to the first referred to activity. Therefore I suggest that in respect of this $2,500,000, there is complete control, which did not obtain in connection with these transactions in 1939.

What were the
controls in 1939?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There was not sufficient control. That is, the operations had been going on from 1935, with applications coming in from year to year. I explained all this to the committee this afternoon, before the hon. member entered the chamber. The applications came in for so many hundreds of operations in 1935, and as I remember it, only about one-quarter of them were completed. The others were carried into 1936. So many applications were received in 1936, and only part of them completed; the remainder were carried into 1937, and so on, until 1938 and 1939. Then in 1938 and 1939, because we partly were paying six cents a cubic yard, and because contractors found they could make money at that rate, particularly if the farmers gave them $25 in addition, the contractors constructed large numbers of dug-outs. The result was that before we discovered that we were likely to have an overexpenditure, the amounts had run into the figures indicated in the auditor general's report.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In other words, the thing got out of hand.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is the position. As soon as it did get out of hand, we stopped the procedure, and placed in effect regulations which are now in control and which, I am quite certain, will prevent a repetition from now on.
With regard to land utilization, and just by way of explanation of what the auditor general says, I would point out that the treasury office now reports an error in its calculations of the overcommitment in land utilization, upon which the auditor general presumably based his notes. The amount, instead of being $22,036.47, is $3,797.80.
From what is the minister reading?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is important, before we proceed further, that I should give details of just what the bill intends to do. The division of voluntary services is responsible for the administration of the War Charities Act. When the act was first drawn, it was not undter War Services. The intention now is to amend it to state that "minister" means the Minister of National War Services. The object of this bill is to provide a measure of control and regulation of the voluntary efforts of organizations throughout Canada in their desire to raise money for war charitable purposes. Under the act any organization which makes an appeal to. the public for donations or subscriptions in money or in kind for any war charity fund or which attempts to do so by sponsoring a bazaar or any other entertainment for that purpose must be registered under the act. That is the provision as it has operated down to the present. Since this act was assented to on September 13, 1939, and- up to May 7, 1941, 1,037 central funds have been registered. In addition, there are 751 branch funds, which have been registered- under a central fund. During the above period the registration of sixty-six funds has been cancelled, and seventy-seven have expired, leaving a net of 1,645 which have been dealt with under the act. The great majority of applications come from responsible groups or organizations. That is, it is not very often that an application has to be refused. They are usually responsible organizations.
After investigation, certificates are issued to such organizations. Then, each application which is not approved, after an investigation, is cancelled and refused. Every effort has been made to prevent the commercializing of war charity efforts. We are finding that in some instances a high percentage of the money taken in entertainments, balls, and so forth, is consumed by expenditures. Where that is found to be the situation it is checked up with the organization, before further permits are given; and if the promoters are not able to satisfy the organiza-

tion that they are going to carry on the ball, or the entertainment, or whatever it may be, in a manner which will secure for war purposes by far the greater part of the money taken in, then there is usually some objection.
According to the War' Charities Act, all organizations registered under the act must make financial returns of their operations to the Department of National War Services, as of March 31 in each year. All of these returns are not as yet in for last year, but the department keeps after them until they finally send the returns in.
The collection of those which have been received up to date total $20,450,000. These figures include the figures for the Red Cross, but they do not include the $6,751,000 raised in the recent campaign for the Canadian war services fund. These figures do, however, include whatever sums organizations in the Canadian war services fund may have raised for the year 1940. Those would be amounts outside the united campaign.
A great many letters dealing with these different drives come to the department from time to time. I have before me the particulars of the last drive, namely, that for the war services, under the direction of Senator McRae. I am afraid I have not those figures before me. I would point out, however, that the amounts were arranged by each of the organizations submitting its budget to a board. That board, headed by Mr. Burton, reduced, the budget considerably, part of the reduction being made in costs of collection. As, however, the figures I have indicated show, every part of Canada went over its objective. Therefore there is a considerable sum-I believe it is about $1,500,000 or $1,600,000-which is now in a special fund, under the direction of a trust board set up to handle that fund. maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In the last war this country had what was known as a patriotic fund. It consisted of moneys subscribed by municipalities, provinces, and private individuals. The day after this war was declared, this country adopted the statute of 1939, which dealt with moneys collected. It would seem that that is now being extended to war supplies.
The minister has said that the united war charities collected about $6,750,000, such moneys to be used by the Y.M.C.A., the Y.W.C.A., the Salvation Army, the Canadian Legion, the I.O.D.E. and the Knights of Columbus. The Red Cross is not included, although I understand it is to take part in the next drive.
I would point out that there are many organizations in the municipalities collecting money from tag days. In addition to that, there are some provincial funds. In this expansion of the War Charities Act, is it the intention to take care of those minor and local agencies, or are they just subsidiaries? I may say there is a wonderful fund, known as the Telegram British war victims fund. I doubt if any fund has done more to educate the people of Canada with regard to the great danger confronting the world and civilization at the present time than this great fund so cheerfully subscribed to all over, at not a cent's cost to the subscribers. That fund should not be interfered with in any way; it is registered, and is a blessing. It is doing great pioneer work, and I am glad to see that it is not interfered with by the new act. It is a separate organization. The war charities board that has been appointed under this bill comprises good citizens, and their first year's work has been well done, but I suggest to the minister that the time has come when the government should make a free, substantial contribution to the mother country in food, clothing and equipment of all kinds. Why could we not make a gift to the people there of grain, butter, and all kinds of food, clothing, and many other commodities that are not covered by the agriculture agreements which the minister has made with the mother country? Further, I suggest that any contributions of that sort and free gifts should be made immediately.
The other day I received a letter from two Canadian soldiers in a village in England. The place was bombed, and among the sufferers was a woman who had lost two sons and her husband. One of the soldiers who wrote to me asked this lady what she would like and she replied, "Oh, if I could only get two pounds of sugar and a pound of butter!"
There is in that reply a principle involved. Why not give this help and these free offerings? Are we or are we not at this time doing
War Charities Act

our full duty to the mother country? We can get the ships, but I do not think we are contributing many of the things that we could very well afford to send over to the old countiy as a gift. For instance, butter is badly needed. Under this particular section of war munitions and war supplies the government itself could collect and send over, weekly or monthly, as a voluntary gift, a large quantity of supplies from the people of Canada. I hope that this new fund of the war charities board will be a success. The work done by that board so far has been most commendable and well done, and I understand that the Red Cross is willing to join in the next drive. In any event, it is to be hoped that the element of time for the next drive will be considered carefully by the minister, because there is bound to be a conflict among these various loan and other appeals to the public. Many organizations and private individuals collecting locally are apt to come into collision, and I hope that every possible step wiir be taken to see that their activities are harmonized, and that the time will be arranged by the government.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I understood there was a difference of opinion between the minister and the Red Cross officials in Saskatchewan in connection with the proposed drive. How was it finally settled?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The matter to which the hon. member refers was brought up in the house in the early part of the session. There really was not a difference of opinion between the Saskatchewan group and the minister, but there was a misunderstanding in the organization itself. That difference has been entirely ironed out within the organization. The proposal made at the time the united drive was organized was to the effect that if the Red Cross desired more money to carry on through this year, they should come into the drive which took place in March and ask for more money from the public at that time. They thought, or at any rate some of their officials thought, they would probably be able to get through this year without appealing for additional money, and they so intimated. I understand that later the Red Cross did conclude that if they were to do certain work which some of them suggested ought to be done, they would require more money. That question has been under discussion since, and it has been pretty well determined that if it is decided to go on with that particular work, some means will have to be found of obtaining money for the purpose. Whether that will be done by a limited collection, or how it will be done, has not yet been decided, but the

spirit of the decision made some time ago is being carried out by the Red Cross and by everyone concerned.
At the moment the Red Cross is considering the question whether it will go into one united drive later on. As a matter of fact, it has indicated a willingness to do so. I would not say that it has been definitely decided that there will be only one drive, but the intention is that there shall be only two drives in the year. One will be in the early part of the year to raise funds for auxiliary war services, that is to say, all matters having to do with charities in connection with the war or auxiliary work in camps. The other, it is expected, will be held in the later part of the year and will cover many of the matters referred to by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who discussed many of these other activities that are going on. It is hoped that they will all be brought into the second united drive, so that there will be only two main national drives in the year.

speechtext:
What
