speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
A committee is proposed in the act. It has not yet been constituted, but we have auditors who check the accounts of these organizations, or have the accounts

War Chanties Act
sent in to be checked. In my first explanation of the bill I should have said that the most important feature is contained in the definition of "war charities' fund," and the provisions that are made to enforce it. "War charities' fund" now means any fund having for its object or among its objects any purpose, charitable or otherwise, arising out of or connected with the war. It is not intended now that only those raising money for charitable purposes should come to this branch of the department, but any organization that is collecting money for any purpose from the public, and having to do with the war, must apply for a permit in order to make its collection, and its books will be subject to examination by the department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Does that apply to small undertakings in procuring comforts for the local camps?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext: It is intended to apply more particularly to the raising of funds for Spitfires and all that sort of thing-probably one hundred or two or three hundred thousand dollars.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Has the department considered awarding a decoration in the form of a ribbon, or a diploma, or a card of honour, to the associations throughout the country which have been doing such splendid work in knitting and gathering together comforts of one kind or another and sending them either through the Red Cross or directly to the boys overseas? In the last war a great deal of the same work was done by many organizations, and after the war some recognition was given to the occasional one. But down the ladder among the ordinary people in the towns and cities very little recognition, if any, was given to the many groups of ladies who did that kind of work. I always thought that the authorities failed in recognition of the vast amount of voluntary service that was given.
Since the present war commenced, I know that in my own riding the Davenport Conservative ladies under the chairmanship of Mrs. S. H. Gillson meet weekly in a room that is donated to them for the purpose, with heat and so forth, and there they sit all afternoon knitting and sewing and making comforts, which, when received overseas, are, I am sure, greatly appreciated. In fact, I have seen many letters that have come back expressing that appreciation.
The hon. member for Broadview mentioned another case of splendid work. He did not elaborate on it, and I think I should say a further word about the Toronto Telegram which has done wonderful service, which has
cost that newspaper a large sum of money. Every dollar contributed to the Telegram war victims' fund goes to the Lord Mayor of London's fund. I believe the amount is now on the way to a million dollars and the work is continuing. The Telegram has done a marvellous work not only in connection with that fund but in creating, especially in the cities and towns of Ontario, in the schools, lodges, churches and organizations of one kind and another, a patriotic spirit that is most commendable and that I do not believe would have prevailed to the same extent but for the great work that newspaper is doing. The space that it is giving to the fund, if estimated in advertising dollars, would amount to a large sum. It also pays the full cost of the bookkeeping and collecting of that fund and sending it overseas.
As I listened this evening, I wondered whether the minister had in mind the bringing about of some means of giving fitting honour and recognition to organizations that do this sort of work. I am not speaking of the Telegram particularly; it may not want anything like that; but any organization that does such work is surely entitled at least to a letter of thanks from the government, and not only from this government but from the government in the old country.
Personally I have been thrilled by the work the minister has developed. He took over a new department, organized the programme and I think on the whole has done a very good job that has resulted in much comfort to the men overseas and in the conservation of a large amount of material which otherwise would have gone to waste. The minister I believe deserves the thanks of the committee for organizing this new department and doing what he has done.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Mackenzie made some reference to a misunderstanding between the Saskatchewan Red Cross and the department; that is, some publicity has been given through the press to an alleged misunderstanding. Following the last war the Saskatchewan Red Cross continued its activities, established outposts in what might be called Saskatchewan's hinterland, and likewise maintained a nursing service. It has rendered invaluable service to the remoter parts of Saskatchewan. In addition, the Red Cross established a children's hospital which it has maintained since that time and has done a magnificent work. In the last fiscal year the Saskatchewan Red Cross raised approximately $696,000, which is not too bad for one organization operating in what is popularly known as the dust-bowl or the
War Chanties Act

drought area of Saskatchewan. In that time they have organized some 800 branches, which function largely through the agency of women's organizations, and in addition to money contributions they have done much in the way of providing comforts for the soldiers. Notwithstanding their disappointment at the inability or unwillingness of the department to consent to a second campaign in 1941, they threw themselves, as an organization and as individuals affiliated with the Red Cross, wholeheartedly into the campaign for national war services, with the result that our province of Saskatchewan more than doubled its quota. I am sure that under the Minister of National War Services there will be no misunderstanding, and that much will be done to harmonize and keep intact the splendid Red Cross organization which has been built up in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Six charities have joined in the national campaign this year. I gather that it will be the policy of the government to increase that number and get more warrantable charities working together in these two campaigns. That being the situation, I should like to know what effect that policy will have on those districts where it has been the custom to join together locally, choosing their own war charities, campaigning in an appeal which shall be the only appeal for those six or twelve months, and making their own allocation. Will it be the policy of the government to attempt to do away with those efforts and substitute for them this national effort?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Our first intention was to build from those organizations which were in existence in many cities across Canada and gradually to bring Canada into one united effort in connection with, first, war services and then, as separate from that, the civil charities. We found, however, that was going to be too slow, and therefore we brought the organizations together with the idea of having a united drive arranged from the top down rather than from the bottom up. That was necessitated by certain conditions which arose in connection with financing. We had to raise much larger sums than we figured we might in the early stages. I think the only way the plan can operate successfully is for the different organizations enumerated of the group doing war auxiliary services, the names of which I have already read, and adding thereto the Red Cross, to keep in a group by themselves. All are groups that are actually doing war service either in the camps in Canada or at the battle front. The idea is to keep these organized in that way but to induce every organization interested in collecting funds to put forth its efforts to assist in collecting the money. After all, it is 
just about the same people who do the collecting all across Canada, irrespective of what appeal is being made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I think they change the personnel of the organization, but they collect from pretty much the same people.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext: In most communities practically the same people will go out in the fall and collect for home charities. At another time, perhaps the same people will go out and put on a drive in order to collect funds for war charities, all under the auspices of this same organization. It is found that in some cities there are organizations purely local in nature, which do not extend to other cities, at least under the same name. Those organizations are interested in some work being carried on in their particular communities. I have in mind cities such as Montreal, for example, where certain organizations carry on work that is not done in other parts of Canada. Those organizations would hardly be considered national. They are doing work that is similar to certain national activities, but it is under different auspices.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I understand some $6,751,630 was collected in the first appeal under the war charities fund, but I should like to know whether it is intended in the next appeal to seek subscriptions from the municipalities and provinces as was done in the patriotic fund during the last war. I believe that was not done this time. This war charities board has done a splendid job in coordinating this charitable work and avoiding and saving duplication and overhead, and it must be remembered that this war is far different from the last so far as the collection of this money is concerned. Then I should like to know whether various local sporting bodies throughout the country that collect sporting equipment and other material for use by the troops in various local camps will come under this legislation, and whether it will be considered essential that they should register and take out permits.
There is one other question I wish to ask in connection with the parcels being sent overseas by the various organizations coming under this fund. These parcels are sent to the old country, to other theatres of war, and to Germany. I believe all the parcels sent to the old country by the post office are delivered, with the exception of those lost as a result of enemy action; but according to the British Hansard of a few months ago that is not the situation with regard to parcels: sent to Germany. We must remember that there are a number of Canadian prisoners of war in Germany, and I was surprised to learn

War Charities Act
recently that there are thousands of women, a few of them Canadians, who are prisoners of war there as well. It was said in the British house that by reason of the difficulties in Spain, through which parcels were routed from Lisbon to Germany, a great many of these parcels have been lost, and at that time some eleven members that I named last February, of the British house asked the government several questions with regard to the delivery of these British parcels. Can anything be done by the war charities board, or have any rules or regulations been passed by that body, with reference to the sending of parcels to Germany for Canadians through the seven bodies included in this bill; and, if so, what are those rules or regulations? It seems to me that if the British Red' Cross cannot deliver these parcels, it must be doubly difficult for these other organizations to do so, although the Canadian Red Cross reply that they do deliver them. They are all doing splendid work; I intend no criticism of them at all, but I should like to know if any rules or regulations have been adopted by the government or the board with regard to the delivery of parcels to prisoners of war, and I would ask the minister to take up the matter with the board and have some inquiry made into it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
My understanding is that the only way in which parcels can be delivered to prisoners of war in Germany is through the International Red Cross, and that the regulations in that respect were drawn up at Geneva. We had nothing to do with the drawing up of those regulations. As a matter of fact, that is one activity which the Red Cross now consider they may have to enlarge, compared with what they have been doing recently. The larger the number of prisoners of war in Germany, the greater and the more expensive will become that work; but it is all carried out under international regulations which were framed at Geneva, and the Red Cross organization is expected to do that work.
In answer to the other question, as to those who will have to apply for permits, as the legislation is now drafted all organizations collecting money for war purposes come under the act and will have to apply for permits to proceed.

maintopic: WAR CHARITIES ACT, 1939 AMENDMENTS TO COVER FUNDS RAISED FOR PURCHASE OF WAR SUPPLIES, ETC.

For one year he worked with Detroit Creamery Farms, Detroit, Michigan, as herdsman in charge of the herd on the state fair circuit and in charge of the Michigan state herd at the national dairy show, 1925. He then joined the staff of the dominion experimental station at Lethbridge under Doctor W. H. Fairfield, where he was in charge of live stock and dry land cultural investigations from March, 1925, until March, 1930. From 1930 until 1935 he was engaged in practical agriculture. During his period of practical farming he had interesting experience with stock on mineral deficient soils in northern Saskatchewan and with large scale farming, alfalfa production and stock raising in southern Alberta. In 1935 he joined the staff of the dominion live stock branch, and was with them until about a year ago. In my opinion Mr. Newman was a valuable member of the department, and I should appreciate very much having the minister make a statement as to why a member of his staff with such a valuable record should not have been retained in the department. Mr. Newman was performing a valuable piece of work, and surely there must be something wrong with the department when a man with a record such as his cannot be retained in the service.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As I understand the situation, Mr. Newman left the department of his own accord. There was no objection to him, in so far as the department was concerned, but he decided that he would like to leave the department and take up other work. I understand he is now doing some organization work in Alberta. The department did not desire him to quit; I understand he just left of his own accord.

He did leave, but it was understood that more responsible work would be given to him. I think the committee is entitled to a fuller explanation than the minister has given. This correspondence would indicate that he did not leave the department willingly or without giving the matter a good deal of thought. I think this department should make greater effort to retain men doing the type of work Mr. Newman was doing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who is the present director?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No one has been appointed to take his place.
I should like the minister to give a fuller explanation. .

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The only fuller explanation I can give is that he thought he should be made permanent at an earlier date, which would, of course, carry with it an increased salary. He was not made permanent, and he left the service of the department.

The correspondence
indicates that Mr. Newman gave up a good position with the McIntyre ranch in southern Alberta when he was persuaded to come to the department on the understanding that he would receive a permanent position in the course of a reasonable time. I understand he was with the department five years and still had not received any assurance that he would receive a permanent appointment. I think the department should be able to determine, in five years whether a man of this sort could be given a permanent position. There must have been some reason for keeping him off the permanent staff. This is a matter of considerable importance, and we should have a fuller explanation.

This is not Doctor
Newman, the dominion cerealist, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. If my hon. friend insists upon an explanation, the only thing I can say is that the department did not think it necessary to urge him any further to remain.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
15. Production service. Health of animals- administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act and Meat and Canned Foods Act, $1,652,495.

What success is the department having in stamping out contagious diseases among animals? The details on page 63 of the estimates show a great number of veterinary inspectors, and I should like to know if it is necessary to have 200 or so of these inspectors in this branch. Could not this number be cut down considerably?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There has been considerable pressure in recent years for the examination of cattle for tuberculosis, one of the reasons being the fact that animals shipped to the United States, where most of our surplus cattle go, must be examined unless they are to be slaughtered shortly after arrival. Many of the areas where dairy cattle are raised are insisting upon examinations being made. We have had to cut down considerably this year on these activities, and have had to reduce the amount of money available for this service, compared with two or three years ago. We should like to have more money to spend in order to clean up all districts.
The province of Ontario is insisting strongly on having many districts which have not yet been covered brought in. We have to go on

Supply-Agriculture
and do the work in the districts that have been covered already, at least once and, in some instances, twice. We are not able to cut down on the staff immediately we start to discontinue bringing in counties because we must complete the work and reexamine cattle. At the moment, however, an effort is being made to reduce rather than to increase the expenditures on this work.

I hope the minister will
find it possible to continue this work and expand the areas. The farmers in the smaller areas suffer a great disadvantage when it comes to selling their cattle. They find they cannot ship cattle unless they have been passed. Just a few miles south of me is an area into which cattle cannot be shipped unless they have been tested for tuberculosis. We understood at the time that a very large area was going to be taken in, but the department decided not to extend that area, and we are now under the difficulty of not being able to bring in stock from outside unless it is tested. It has been necessary to quarantine stock for six weeks and two months before they could be brought into that area, and that causes a great deal of difficulty and inconvenience. I hope the government will extend that area as rapidly as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: One of the difficulties in Alberta is that it was only three or four years ago at the outside that Alberta made their first request for an area to be taken in. Prior to that time, the government or the people of Alberta did not see fit to come under the act. Other provinces were coming in. The maritimes-I am speaking from memory- are completely covered, also a large part of the other two prairie provinces, and a large part of Ontario and Quebec, but Alberta did not start to come under the act until three or four years ago, and the area there is not as large as in some of the other provinces. I am soriy that the war has necessitated our cutting down on bringing in any new territory.

In Ontario, how many
areas have been taken in, and is it the intention to clean up the areas already in?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have a list of those
counties which have applied but have not yet been tested. All the others which have applied have been tested. The counties which have made application but have not yet been examined are Hastings, Haldimand, Lennox-Addington, Dufferin, Huron, Bruce, Haliburton, Oxford, Perth, Wellington, Middlesex and Elgin. All the other counties which have made application have been examined at least once or are in the stage of going through the test for the first time. It is the intention of
the department to clean up these counties if we can obtain sufficient funds from year to year, and we intend to clean these up before taking in any new areas.

A great many farmers
feel that once an area has been tested, the work should be carried on if at all possible.

How many areas are there
in Saskatchewan?	'

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: How many is that?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: About thirty-five.
Is it not a fact that Saskatchewan is the healthiest province as regards not only human beings but animals as well?

I should like to compliment the department upon this expenditure. I wish it were a little larger. I would also draw the attention of the committee, particularly members of the medical profession, to the fact that this item calls for an expenditure of $1,652,495 to take care of the health of the animals of Canada. In comparison with that, I should like them to note the total estimates to look after the health of the human beings of Canada. They amount to $1,011,605.
That is from the dominion government only.
The provincial governments have health departments, it is true, but I believe the federal department of health should extend its work.

Has the health of animals branch made any investigation with regard to calf-hood vaccination for Bangs disease? This disease works greater ravages among cattle than even tuberculosis. I do not know whether the disease can be passed on to human beings as easily as tuberculosis. I have been led to believe that considerable experimenting has been done in the United States which would indicate that they have something there that is worth while, and I should like to know whether our department here is prepared to provide the serum for the prevention of Bangs disease and whether any investigation has been made into calf-hood vaccination.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The department has made investigations. We do not do this work directly but have undertaken, wherever any province desires to have it carried on in the province, to provide cultures with which to carry it on.

Supply-Agriculture

I should like to say a few words in reply to the remark of the hon. member for Yorkton. In all probability this work under health of animals branch would not be done at all if it were not for the fact that tuberculosis in cattle can be carried to human beings. All our activities in connection with contagious diseases in cattle are carried on because cattle and milk are used as human food. Therefore it is all part and parcel of the one job.

In certain districts in the west probably 70 per cent of individual herds have been tested. Is there any provision in the act whereby when a certain percentage, say 75 per cent, of the herds in an area have been tested, that area would automatically become a tuberculous-free area and the remainder of the herds be cleaned up?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No. That condition
may arise, but it is not accepted as a reason for making it an area. All the herds in the area must be checked by veterinaries and tested for tuberculosis before the area itself is called an anti-tuberculosis area.

I rise to commend the
minister upon the suggestion to proceed with the cleaning up of counties which have already been listed. I should also like to bring to his attention the county of Hali-burton. The county of Victoria, just south of Haliburton, has already been cleaned up, and I believe the same applies to Ontario on the west and Peterborough on the east. The cattle population of Haliburton county is not extensive, but it serves as a source of supply of stocker cattle for Ontario, Victoria and Peterborough. It entails a substantial amount of work on the part of veterinaries serving that area to take care of the rush of stocker cattle which come down at certain seasons of the year. If at all possible, I think it would facilitate matters very much in the four counties I have mentioned, if that area could be cleaned up with as little delay as possible. Such action would greatly improve the supply of milk so essential for the important tourist business of this area.

I do- not wish to take
issue with what has been said by the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario. Nevertheless, I come from a county where the subject of the tubercular test is a keen one. We in that county import from the west great numbers of stocker cattle. If pressure is brought to bear on the county of Middlesex to have the tubercular test, it will mean great hardship on the men who import those stocker cattle from the west.

Which part of the
west?

Saskatchewan and
Alberta.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
IS. Production service. Compensation for animals slaughtered, $530,000.
How much has been paid out in compensation?

Would the minister give
the figures by provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The amount paid out
since the beginning was $13,201,979. The amount paid in 1939-40 was $836,875.33. I have not the amounts by provinces.
At what rate is the compensation paid?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The amount to be paid is two-thirds of the valuation. The highest valuation that can be put on grades is $60, and the highest on pure-bred cattle is $150.
How much was paid out for hog cholera?

The total amount last
year was S202.000. The total up to that time, for all preceding years, was $724,569.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
17. Production service. Live stock and poultry, $707,597.55.

I believe I am
entitled to express my views to the minister. In my constituency the farmers are engaged in either dairying, small fruit farming, or poultry raising. The position in which the poultry farmer of the Fraser valley finds himself is one in which it is absolutely impossible for him to carry on. Hundreds of thousands of their stock have had to be slaughtered, because they could not afford to produce under present production costs, and at present selling prices.
I have secured my information from the bureau of statistics, and from an equally well-known authority in respect of telephone and other rates, namely, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I believe he has no equal in respect of information concerning freight rates.
At the present time my constituency, and the province of British Columbia, must depend upon export rates because, roughly speaking, our price is based on the export rate received for nine-tenths of our production. That means, obviously, that the domestic rate applies to only one-tenth. I am speaking particularly to farmer members, although I am sorry there are not more in the house. I am glad, however, to see a few members of the legal

Supply-Agriculture
fraternity who happen to represent farming districts. So far as British Columbia is concerned, I would point out that we must receive at least the cost of production, and that in the last year we have not received that much.
I would point out particularly to my hon. friends to the left that agriculture in Canada is not tied up completely with the word "wheat". With all due deference, I would point that out to the Minister of Agriculture. Wheat is only a by-product of agriculture in Canada.
It is good poultry feed.
All right, now; I do not mind these interruptions from these small wheat farmers.
I do not think the Minister of Agriculture should allow that to go unchallenged.

I know, from my past experience, that the Minister of Agriculture is quite capable of looking after himself. We are not getting paid-and I repeat it- for ploughing under our chickens. Last year on the average we received only sixteen and three-quarter cents a dozen for eggs in British Columbia. I do not believe the minister knew that, or that his departmental officials knew it. If they did, then they did1 not bring it to his attention. I repeat that sixteen and three-quarter cents a dozen was the average price the poultrymen in British Columbia were paid in 1940 for their eggs. It is all right for the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, because he will continue to plough under his wheat when I am through with these eggs.
An hon. member from Ontario has mentioned that egg production in British Columbia continues the year round. Any farmer member should know that production from poultry is greater from March to June. I am surprised there are not more practical farmers in the house.
In British Columbia our price is set entirely by the export rate, nine-tenths of which is for export purposes and only one-tenth for domestic consumption; and in order to get into the export market we have to ship to Montreal, Halifax or Saint John. For freight purposes bacon is put in class 4 and eggs in class 5, and both commodities are shipped in exactly the same type of refrigerator car. For the first time in my life I took some notes that cannot be disputed. There is this discrimination. I would point out to the minister and his efficiency experts that apples and eggs are shipped by the same type of transportation. A crate of eggs is 56 pounds and a box of apples 50 pounds, and the type of car is the same. Taking our two colossal insti-
14873-218J
tutions, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways, we find that the freight to Halifax and Saint John on apples is $1.29 per hundred pounds, minimum of 37,500-pound car, and eggs from British Columbia to Halifax and Saint John have a rate of $2.10 per hundred pounds, minimum of 40,000-pound car. I do not pretend to speak for all hon. members from British Columbia, but I certainly can claim to speak for the rural riding of Fraser Valley, and I say that while we have never questioned the right of the prairie farmer to a fair price for his wheat, a price that will give him cost of production, we ask for the same consideration from them and from the minister. We want to get cost of production so far as eggs are concerned.
A short time ago we applied to the government for some consideration with regard to the price of butter, and we advanced an argument to show how in our opinion the price could be arrived at. We realized that a contract had to be carried out with the old country in connection with cheese and suggested that it might be necessary to subsidize the price of that commodity in the ratio known in the ordinary farming district as two and a half to one so as to equalize matters in order to allow us to produce cheese. I am glad that the government has done that. At the same time I urge that something be done along the same line for the protection of the poultryman.
I give credit to the government for having reduced the rate on mixed grains, which were supposed to be used as feed for poultry on western farms and, I presume, in the mari-times. But let me point out to the minister, and particularly to his advisers, something that they have not realized, so far as British Columbia is concerned. Within two weeks of that rate being put into effect, the feed companies increased their price on feed from one to two dollars, and not one word was said by the price-fixing board. These facts can be verified by the department. We appreciate the so-called concession on mixed grains to the Pacific coast, but of what advantage is that to us when the feed companies immediately increase their price to the producer from one to two dollars a ton? The same applies to grain of all kinds-bran and shorts or mixed grains. Speaking for the largest poultry producing area in British Columbia, I say it is time the department stepped in. If you can say to the Ford Motor company or to General Motors, "You shall get a fair return on a gun carrier, bren-gun carrier, universal carrier or whatever it is called", then you can say to the poultry producer, "You shall get a fair return on the commodities you produce."
Supply-Agriculture

The price has been fixed on butter and wheat, and I commend the government in both instances because the price was too low. We have at least guaranteed an equitable return to the producers of apples in the east and in the west, and last year and again this year we have guaranteed a return to the fisherman for his lobster catch. Eggs happen to be one of the commodities of which Great Britain is much in need, and I suggest that a minimum return should be guaranteed the producer. At least he should get cost of production. With regard to this item now under consideration, amounting to over 1700,000, I should like to know whether any provision is made therein to see that the poultry producer in British Columbia, who must be guided in his prices by the export market, will be protected in exactly the same way as the apple grower and the .butter and cheese producer-.

I would ask members of the committee to be good enough to turn to page 65 of the estimates, which gives details of this item. They will see the absurdity of the classifications of the civil service commission. There is an expert, a B.S.A., who is in charge of the whole Department of Agriculture, Post Office and some other things, and he is crazy-and this does not appear in Hansard, nor is it in the statute book. I hope, however, that hon. members who have page 65 in front of them will take the trouble to follow me as I go through it. In the first place, there is one assistant director, production service, live stock who receives $4,920. Then there is one chief, live stock and poultry production services, $4,140. Then there are two associate chiefs, live stock and poultry production services, one at $3,660 and one at $3,510, or a total of $7,170. There is a chief registration officer at $3,660. Then there is one assistant chief, poultry production services -all services in connection with poultry-at $3,450, and there is another assistant chief, live stock and poultry production services, who has another job-not, perhaps, all poultry production services. It is live stock and poultry production services. Therefore he is more responsible than the man who looks after only the hens, roosters and chicks. He looks after live stock, big bulls and cows, and yet he gets less money, $270 per annum less than the man who only looks after hens and chicks. This must have been decided at Easter.
Then there is a district supervisor, live stock and poultry production services, at $3,300. The district supervisor has a little more than the assistant chief. Then there are the district live stock field men, one at

$3,240, one at $3,000; and three supervising live stock field men, one at $2,880, one at $2,820 and one at $2,790. The supervising live stock field men are paid less than the district live stock field men, and the district live stock field man is better paid than the assistant chief, live stock and poultry production services.
What I say is not Greek; it is the kind of classification made by these so-called experts whom I call fools. I want the committee to realize that these so-called experts are fools, hon. members have it here and can check it for themselves.
Then there is a chief record of performance inspector at $3,000; three live stock production assistants at $2,760; sixteen senior live stock field men, one at $2,760, ten at $2,520, one at $2,490, one at $2,280 and one at $2,220. There is a senior poultry field man. That is an important position, it is like a decoration, S.P.F.M.; he gets $2,340. There is one principal clerk, and there are five live stock field men, two at $1,920, one at $1,860 and one at $1,845, a difference of $15, and one at $1,665. I find that a man must be very able to appreciate the services of two live stock field men and mark a difference of salary of $15 per annum. Joe has $15 per annum more than Tom. It shows how meticulously careful they are and how well they do things. If the one who received $1,845 had received $1,860, it would be theft because he would not have earned it!
Then there is a supervising record of performance inspector at $1,920. He should not be confounded with the chief record of performance inspector who receives $3,000. This is a much lower job. There are poultry field men at lower salaries, and record of performance inspectors who must not be confounded with the supervising record of performance inspector and clerks and stenographers and so forth. I know there are some doctors in the Department of Agriculture, I Wonder whether the fellow who prepared these specifications is also a doctor. But I find it the greatest absurdity. Mark you, I do not blame the minister for that; it is the system, and I think the organization branch of the civil service commission should be abolished. It is only jealousy; there is no reason for all sorts of types being together on the same page in this way.
To conclude with a practical question; I would remind the minister that during those dark days when R. B. Bennett was Prime Minister, nearly all the bilingual propagandists of his department were fired. How many propagandists are there now? I hope the minister will be kind enough to answer the

Supply-Agriculture
question. I shall be thankful to him for telling us how many more are there now than when the Bennett government was defeated?
May I have an answer to my question?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I did not have an opportunity to answer before my hon. friend on this side was on his feet, but I would suggest that the proper place to discuss what my hon. friend was bringing up is under marketing. I have not here the officials to whom my hon. friend would like to address his remarks, but I shall have the information a little later to cover some of the points raised.
As to the questions raised by the hon member for Temiscouata, while there may be some things that are not exactly right in connection with the classifications they are not as foolish as he would have them appear. For example, take the assistant director of production services; the salary range in that classification is from $4,320 to $4,920, the increases being at the rate of $300 a year. Therefore an individual who comes in at the bottom of the classification, at the end of the first year goes up $300; next year, up another $300, and so on. It is possible that in going down the list of individuals one could take a man in his first year, compare him with one at the top of the list and say that it is difficult to justify the difference. Then another classification runs from $3,7S0 to $4,140; the next from $3,300 to $3,660, and the next from $3,000 to $3,240. There is some relationship between the classifications, but if one compares a man at the bottom with one at the top of the same classification, it might give a wrong impression.

I should like to
have my question straightened out. Under what section would it come?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Marketing comes under
items 22 to 28; live stock and live stock prodi-ucts is item 27; dairy products, item 24. Marketing service administration, under which general discussion of marketing would come, is item 22.
With all due respect to the hon. member for Temiscouata, I am not particularly interested in how much an individual receives so long as he gets results. But I point out that item 22-

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We are still on item 17.

I was trying to
expedite matters. The minister pointed out that my question would be covered by a certain item and-
The hon. member's question, I understand, comes under item 22, marketing service administration, to item 27.

I point out that
item 22 does not include enough money, and therefore I shall have to ask to be permitted to explain myself a little more fully.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think I understand what the hon. member has in mind, that the amount of money provided is not sufficient to cover what he is suggesting, namely, an increase in the price of eggs from sixteen to, say, twenty cents. Those steps are not taken under these estimates at all. The action in connection with the price of cheese, for example, and the price of hogs-and the action in connection with the price of eggs if that should .be taken-is taken under the War Measures Act, and the money involved is paid out of the appropriation under that act where we are dealing with a condition that has arisen as a result of the war. There is not enough money in any of these items to deal with matters of that kind.

I thank the minister for understanding what I had in mind when I said this was not enough money. Is there any estimate under which the minister will be able to tell me later on whether or not the money will be available to increase the price of eggs as well as the price of cheese?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It will be quite proper
to discuss all marketing matters under the marketing estimates, in spite of the fact that the money is>
not provided under those estimates. The administration of those sums comes under those items; the individuals who are administering the expenditure of the money come under items 22 to 28, and it would be quite proper to discuss that matter then.

There is one other point on which I differ with the hon. member for Temiscouata. I am not particularly concerned with the salaries of the administrators. I am interested in the farmers; the administrators can look after themselves. I take it from the minister that there will be an item under which I can obtain some information with regard to what is to happen to the poultryman, who is a war casualty in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Everything having to do with the marketing of poultry, live stock and live stock products may be dealt with under that item.

The minister said that those classifications were not so foolish as I represented them to be. Of course that is a matter
Supply-Agriculture

of opinion. Opinions are free. That is the opinion of the minister. I hold the contrary opinion, but that is my own business. On the other hand, I would very much regret having to take time to show in connection with every item that the classifications of each branch of his department are even more foolish than those to which I have already referred. I could show that to the satisfaction of anyone who has eyes to see and ears to listen.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The hon. member for Temiscouata asked one question to which I did not reply, namely, with regard to the number of bilingual persons employed on these staffs having to do with this branch of the department. There are 134 employees in the outside staff across Canada, .and there are thirty-nine employed in the province of Quebec, all of whom. I understand are bilingual.

I wish it to be distinctly on the record that the member for Fraser Valley has never yet apologized and never will apologize for the magnificent valley he represents. A little over a year ago I had the privilege of having the Minister of Agriculture visit my riding. Possibly if he had not visited the riding I would not be here to-day. I never have been and I never will be a yes-man. If I thought that my farmers were not getting what they were entitled to, I would be ready to say so. The fact that I am a supporter of the government does not mean that I will always agree with the government. Perhaps I know a little more about Canada than some hon. members because I have been in every province with the exception of Prince Edward Island. I have been in twenty-eight of the United States, and I know something of farming and pioneering conditions in different parts of the country. I claim that Chilliwack is the finest farming district in the dominion, even though I do not happen to live there myself.
I should like to take the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) along our main highway as far as the spa of Canada, Harrison Hot Springs, which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) paid us the honour of visiting a short time ago. I would be able to show him that 60 per cent of the farmers along that highway are the class of farmer that my friend mentioned. He did not mention the letterhead on that letter he just
read, but I saw it. He was talking about a city farmer, a rose-bush farmer, a man who never had to make a living off the farm.
At one time he did.

He may have at one time, but not to-day. I should like the hon. member for Renfrew North to show me a farmer in British Columbia with enough money to-day to go out and buy ninety cows. There is not a farmer in my riding with enough cash to do so, and I come from a good riding. I have something in my valley which the hon. member has not in his. I have a farmer who bought SI ,000,000 worth of interest-free bonds in bis own name, and SI,000,000 worth in the name of the company of which he is the president. That is the type of farmer about whom my hon. friend is talking. According to the letterhead, I imagine his friend is doing a very good business with the Department of Munitions and Supply. It is, however, a different proposition when one is really farming.
I can assure my hon. friend that I shall have nothing to say about the farmers in his riding because I know nothing about them. I have never been in his riding. I wish to tell him with all due respect that he has not the faintest knowledge about what he is talking in so far as the farmers of my riding are concerned. I have been compared with the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen). I think yesterday looked after the hon. member for North Battleford. I wish to tell the hon. member for Renfrew North that if he has no more sympathy for the downtrodden fanner than to commend the government for everything it does, whether it is right or wrong, the people of that riding will look after him in the same way as they looked after the hon. member for North Battleford on Monday.
-I have asked for no sympathy from the hon. member for Renfrew North. I know what I am talking about when I speak about my riding. I shall be delighted to have him as my guest. I can show him a millionaire farmer who has his race horses, and another one who has carried on sugar-beet experiments at a possible loss of $40,000, for which I give him credit for experimenting. But he gets that money from oil and other stocks. I am speaking for the farmer who has not these things. I could show the hon. member for Renfrew North a farm in Fraser Valley which is renting for $5.15 an acre when the taxes are $4.88 an acre. He knows nothing of these conditions. Hon. members have never heard me deprecate the value of the minister's own province of Saskatchewan or its needs. I know nothing about wheat, and I know
Supply-Agriculture

nothing about conditions in Renfrew North. But I do know about conditions in Fraser Valley. I know of one municipality of 5,500 people where the relief costs average $4,200 a month. I am told that there are corresponding municipalities in Ontario with an average relief cost of $27. It would bring about more harmony and unity from the agricultural point of view if some of these members from rural Ontario would come out for the farmer who is not getting a fair deal.

The hon. member for Renfrew North was critical of the hon. member for Fraser Valley for his reference to sixteen cents a dozen for eggs and stated that in Ontario he is receiving twenty cents for grade A large. He is fortunate in marketing his eggs in Ontario. In Alberta, grade A large eggs bring to the producers fifteen cents; grade A, medium, fourteen cents; grade B, twelve cents, and grade C, eight cents. Therefore I think the hon. member for Fraser Valley is correct in his argument that prices for eggs are to-day altogether too low; and while the government is considering minimum prices, they might as well extend their activities to poultry. May I ask if this estimate covers the branch which regulates the grading of eggs, or is that a provincial matter?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The last three or four speakers have insisted on discussing marketing. The marketing votes do not start until we get to item 22. If hon. members wish to discuss marketing, I wish they would let us reach the marketing items, when we shall have the officials here and be able to give them all the information they desire.

Does this item refer to
blood-testing?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The details are given on page 65 of the estimates.
Page 65 refers to field men. What do they do? Do they supervise bloodtesting of flocks for hatcheries? Is that a federal responsibility or provincial? *

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is both federal and provincial, but much of that work is carried on by the provinces.
Would the minister explain the item of $154,678 for prizes, bonuses and premiums?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: These are prizes, bonuses and premiums for calf clubs, stallion clubs and clubs of that type existing across the country.
Poultry clubs too?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes; poultry clubs are included in that.
Eggs would come under this item. Will the minister explain the new egg grading regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That all comes under
marketing. How you feed poultry to get good eggs comes under this item, but the grading and selling come under marketing.

This is a production item which has to do with breeding better live stock, poultry and so forth. Having regard to what is going on in the old country and the possibility of destruction of some of their stock or the use for other purposes of their fine bred herds, have any steps been taken by the government or by private individuals to bring foundation stock of some of the better herds to this country since the war broke out?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is some difficulty about bringing out cattle or live stock at present. I did visit a herd during this last week when I was returning from the calf sale of eighteen shorthorn cattle brought out from Scotland very recently. One of the difficulties in bringing out live stock is in establishing quarantine places at the shipping points. In this particular instance the man went ahead and arranged to bring out a certain number. The quarantine place was there at the time, and he managed to get one shipment through. That particular shipment was not of any great advantage to him in what he desired to do, because he was waiting to distribute them through a sale across this country and part of them to the United States. He desired to bring out still more, but in the meantime it had become impossible for him to get a proper quarantine place on the Clyde on account of conditions existing there. There are negotiations going on to tiy to overcome in some way these difficulties, but the war makes it very hard to get stock out without perhaps running into trouble because one might bring over to this country foot-and-mouth disease which would do more harm than any good he might get out of the shipments.

In connection with
foundation herds from the Channel islands, when the Germans occupied the islands a year ago this June or July most of the stock was taken over by the Germans, and the rumour is that it was slaughtered. Fortunately, however, a good percentage had been brought over to this country prior to the invasion, and we have in our constituency on the farm of B. H. Bull and sons a large proportion of the foundation herds of Jersey island. That perhaps may answer the hon. member's question.

Supply-Agriculture

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I remember that the hon. member for Peel asked me a question . in the early part of last session, and I must state that in reply I gave him information which was not entirely correct at that time, although we thought it was correct at the time. Two or three days later it was wrong. Arrangements apparently had been made to take out some of the best bred stock. My memory is that disease broke out and that it was impossible to move the cattle, and they were left there. What happened afterwards it is difficult to say. I imagine that some of them would be slaughtered, and probably disease took care of a good many of them.

Is
the minister doing anything to check the sale of our pure-bred stock to otheT countries? In the last war, in November, 1917, the export of cattle was prohibited from Canadh except to British possessions. After this war we shall have to build up our stock for Europe because their stocks are all slaughtered. The milk for Scotland all comes now from the northern part of Ireland.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We have done nothing yet to prevent the exportation of stock from Canada. While we are on production, I may say that it would appear that we still have very much more live stock of every kind than we had at the beginning of the war. Our production is up in all the different lines, and so far no great harm has come.
Mr.	FRASER	(Peterborough	West):	I
had in mind that people from the south were coming over here, going through our herds and picking out our very best stock for shipment across the line.

They think they do.
Mr.	FRASER	(Peterborough	West):	An
hon. member says, "They think they do". We get a good price for them. We do not wish to discourage this practice altogether- but we should keep some in this country.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
19. Production service. Plant products-seeds feeds,	fertilizers,	insecticides and fungicides
control, including grant of $18,900 to Canadian Seed Growers' Association, $521,642.

I notice it is proposed to spend $521,642 in connection with this item. I have here a large advertisement which	has been	used a good	deal in	the
west. It reads:
Less wheat in 1941 will help win the war. See the secretary of your municipality, he can help you with your application. Published by authority of the Hon. J. G. Gardiner, federal Minister of Agriculture.
Then there are small sheets bearing the words "Less wheat in 1941 will help win the war". Then there is a pink sheet on which appear these words:
Less wheat in 1941 will help win the war. We want hogs; we want butter; we want cheese; we want beef; we need feed. Why grow more wheat than you can sell?
This is also authorized! by the dominion Department of Agriculture. As I pointed out, it is proposed under this vote to spend over half a million dollars for seeds, feeds and fertilizers. Would the minister be good enough to explain why on the one hand we are spending half a million dollars to produce more, while on the other hand we are spending large sums of money to discourage production. It seems to me that the minister might very well cut down this large appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member for Mackenzie is logical in his reasoning. The fact that you cut down wheat for one year does not necessarily mean that you are cutting down production. I do not think anyone would suggest that there is not enough seed wheat in Canada. One might, however, suggest that there are many other seeds of which we have not sufficient quantities. As a matter of fact, we did not have sufficient alfalfa seed, or seeds of any of the other grasses, to distribute throughout western Canada this year in connection with the acreage reduction plan. Much of the grass seed will have to be produced this summer, and seeded in the fall of the year, if farmeirs are going to take advantage of the proposal that they should have more grass next year than they had last year. All of this, of course, is related to the vote for plant products, including seeds, feeds, fertilizers and so forth.
We had difficulty in obtaining sufficient seed oats to seed the land taken out of wheat. We had difficulty in getting sufficient barley. The fact that to a certain extent we were shifting from wheat to other crops made all the more necessary the expenditure of money to provide seed, or to encourage the use of seed. But much of the work which has to be done in connection with seeds and fertilizers has to do with entirely different kinds of crops.
For example, when the war started, many of the seeds we were obtaining for gardening purposes were obtained from countries from which we can now get nothing. We are entirely barred from obtaining seeds of any kind from Holland, Belgium or other European countries. Much of the production of those seeds will have to be developed in this country. As a matter of fact, since the war started, there has been more reason for doing

Supply-Agriculture

work in connection with seed development than there was before. The necessity for it is increasing all the time.
In so far as the advertisements held up to the view of the committee are concerned, I would suggest only this, that while we were discussing the wheat acreage bonus, the leader of the opposition asked me how much I thought would be required, and whether we would use the whole $35,000,000. I told him I did not like to prophesy, but I was not quite optimistic enough to think we would need the whole amount. I wish to say, however, that something induced the farmers to reduce their wheat acreage this year to a degree at least as great as I expected when we started the programme. After all, when one puts out posters and advertisements, he tries to put out something which will be effective. I suggest that something was effective in persuading the farmers to reduce their wheat acreage, when they cut it down to the extent to which it has been cut down.
I believe the wet spring had something to do with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The wet spring might have helped. It is better to have providence with you than against you.
Why must the minister pay analysts' fees when he employs his own chemists? Why can they not do the work?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We have not sufficient
analysts to make all tests required. Then, at times, tests have to be made quickly at places where departmental analysts are not available, and we find it less expensive to use local analysts than to send our men there to do the work.

What is the total amount
paid to analysts, and are there many employed? If there are not too many, I should like to have their names, and the amounts paid to them.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am sorry I have not
the information in that form.

What is done by the
fertilizer branch? What are their duties?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
They do inspection
work. All inspection work to keep fertilizers up to a proper standard is done by this branch of the department. Of course certain work in connection with fertilizers is done by the provinces.

Do they have anything
to do with the regulation of prices?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We have not regulated
the prices. However, when the war started, it was thought there would be some difficulty

in handling fertilizers during the war period, in view of the fact that the war itself, through the manufacturing of munitions, interferes with certain of the ingredients contained in fertilizers. Some control has been taken over fertilizers by the war supply board, but it is not a matter of controlling prices.

Why was the price of
sulphate of ammonia, which forms a large part of fertilizers used in Canada, allowed to increase to the extent of $10 a ton, and why is it held by a monopoly in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The department has
received representations to the effect that the price of sulphate of ammonia has advanced substantially since the commencement of the war, and has referred the matter to the wartime prices and trade board for investigation as to whether or not present prices are justified. Those facts will no doubt be brought out by the investigation. Advance information indicates that, as claimed, the wholesale price of this product, bagged, has increased about $8 a ton. It is now selling at $36, as against $28 at the commencement of the war. The hon. member has said that there has been an increase of $10. The figure I have given may have been secured at a date different from the one he has used.
The reasons given for the advance in price is that manufacturing costs have increased, and the export demand is strong, at prices much higher than present domestic prices. That is the information I have. It has been submitted to the war-time prices and trade board, and we have not yet had their report.

How many manufacturers of sulphate of ammonia are there in Canada? I understand that there are several manufacturers, because it is a by-product from coke ovens. I believe it can be bought only from one firm in Canada; why is that condition allowed?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not in a position to answer the first question. I understand that a number of firms sell sulphate of ammonia, but I have not the information as to the exact number; neither am I informed as to whether it is all sold through one company. I would have to take the hon. member's word for that.

I notice there is an item of $18,900 granted to the Canadian Seed Growers' association. Is that an annual grant, or is there any variation in the grant from year to year. There is an increase of $3,155 in the item. Would the minister explain the

Supply-Agriculture
increase? What was the cost of the advertisement that appeared in the western papers urging farmers to grow less wheat to win the war, and out of what fund was it paid?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have not checked it, but I presume it will be paid out of the amount voted by parliament.
What is the amount?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I cannot say offhand. It would be for printing and the cost of sending out the advertisement. The information was sent to every person, and there are between 200,000 and 300,000 on the mailing list.

This vote has to do with the administration of the Seeds Act, the Feeding Stuffs Act, the Fertilizers Act and the other matters mentioned, but it has no reference at all to the securing of seeds of any kind to seed acreage as suggested to the minister- oats, barley or anything else.
There is one other matter the minister might discuss-the interest taken in the production of fibre flax. I understand that the department has assumed control of the production of that product, and the committee would be interested to know to what degree it has been successful and what the efforts are in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
When the war started, there was considerable agitation to have the production of fibre flax increased, the reason being largely the experience which growers had during the last war. That experience indicated that if the control over seed for the growing of fibre flax was left free, the price would probably rise very high. It might get under the control of one or two individuals and be greatly increased. At the beginning of the war, the agricultural supplies board took control of all fibre flax seed in Canada and distributed that seed at a set price to Ireland and parts of England, retaining in Canada what they thought was sufficient to take care of the requirements of the farmers who would be growing fibre flax here. That seed has been distributed year by year to the different farmers at a set price. For No. 1 certified, it is $6 a bushel; No. 2 certified, $5.25; No. 1 uncertified, $4.25; No. 2 uncertified, $4. The order in council gives the information with regard to the matter, so far as the year 1940 is concerned.	The number of production
centres in Canada totals thirty-five, sixteen being located in Quebec, and nineteen in Ontario. In 1940 the acreage was 22,400, and it is expected that in 1941 it will be over 37,285 acres.	The estimated acreage by
provinces is: In Quebec 25,100; in Ontario, 9,985; in Manitoba, 2,000; in Alberta, 100;
14873-219J
in British Columbia, 100. The total seed requirements for 1941, based on a bushel and a half an acre, amount to 57,000, for which sufficient seed is available, and the exports from the 1940 crop were 22,400 bushels, none of which was certified. Seed distribution was confined this year mainly to those who had facilities for processing the crop, and who applied first for seed. Seed of doubtful breeding was not purchased by the department because this would have meant ruin to the industry in its exports to Ireland. The varieties of fibre flax mainly grown in Canada are Cyrus, Liral, Dominion, Liral Crown, Liral Monarch, Gossamer and J. W. S.
Does the government control production and designate where the fibre flax should be grown?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The department approves the area. It does not exactly pick out areas; but when individuals decide to go into the growing of fibre flax, the department investigates; if the soil and conditions generally are suitable, the areas are approved and the growers go ahead.
Has the department control of all seed?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.

There is an item of
$18,900 for the Canadian Seed Growers' association. What are the names of the members of the board?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The amount voted is the same from year to year, neither increased nor decreased. The association is spread across the country, but it would be difficult to give the names of all those engaged in the various organizations. Mr. Wiener is secretary at Ottawa of the Canadian Seed Growers' association.

Is there a board of
directors?

about twelve men, but I have not the names.

I understand that sulphate of ammonia is a by-product of steel and coke. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I understand so.

If that be so, one would think that since we are making and using twice as much steel since the war, this product should not have gone up in price to the extent of anywhere from $10 to $12 when there is twice the amount available.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member was in his seat when we were dealing with this a few minutes ago. However, there is a piece of information here which I did1 not have before me then. Owing to munition requirements most of the ammonia produced in Canada for the manufacture of sulphate of ammonia is being diverted to the manufacture of explosives. Therefore it is possible that sulphate of ammonia may become scarce in the near future, and a reduction in its use for fertilizer may become necessary. I added that this whole question had been submitted to the war-time prices and trade board, but we have not yet had a report regarding it.
I have not had an answer as to why the fertilizer manufacturers cannot buy sulphate of ammonia from the producers.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I shall have to give to my hon. friend the same answer as before; I do not really know. Probably, however, I can find out. The hon. member states that it can be purchased only from one concern, that there is a monopoly. I imagine that will be inquired into by the war-time prices and trade board.
Are they investigating?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I should think they will be, with regard to price.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
SO. Production service. Grants to fairs and exhibitions, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $65,000.

I think we are cutting down too much our grants to fairs and exhibitions. I realize that there is a war on, but fairs and exhibitions are the show-windows of the pure-bred live stock producer. They are just the same as the show-windows to the large

department stores. This was never more impressed upon me than last fall when I started out to do a little purchasing and visited some pure-bred herds in eastern Ontario. In practically every place they gave as the reason for their stock not looking better that there was no show or fair at which to show their stock, and consequently their sales were down a great deal. It would be a big mistake in connection with our live stock industry to cut down on fairs and shows.

I think the minister has been very fair so far as exhibitions are concerned, but I should like to corroborate what the hon. member for Lanark has said. On the Pacific coast we have developed a wonderful market for pure-bred high-grade stock, both cattle and horses, as far south as San Francisco. The minister has been very fair in the past, and irrespective of the war I think he and the department should take into consideration the future of live stock which is going to be in great demand in Canada. More consideration should be given particularly to class B fairs.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
SI. Production service. Grants to agricultural organizations, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $35,500.

Looking at the details on page 68 of the estimates, grants to agricultural organizations, I notice that $5,000 is granted to the Canadian council on boys' and girls' club work. How is that fund handled and distributed to the different clubs? Also, if I understand this aright, it is the junior calf clubs and so forth, and I am very much in favour of it, and would be in favour of increasing this grant, because a splendid work is being done. In my own province and district a number of these clubs are doing very good work, and the experimental farm at Indian Head provides for the meetings of this club and puts on short courses. Would the minister explain how this money is handled and distributed?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This $5,000 is the grant that is given to the central organization, of which Mr. McLaurin is secretary. The province contributes as well. Our proportion 'is $5,000; it is for the central administrative costs. The .grants which go to groups that gather at exhibitions are contained in the $65,000 item just passed. That is one of the grants to fairs that we did not cut out; we believe that is an important part of the work and should continue right on through the war period.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
