22. Marketing service. Marketing service administration, $95,252.
Under what board does the pegged minimum price on butter come?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Under the dairy products board.
Why is there a provincial board for New Brunswick as well as the dominion board? They are both putting out regulations and prices.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is a provincial board in New Brunswick, and I understand there is talk of trying to organize a board representative of the three maritime provinces, the idea being, as represented to me, that there is a peculiar situation in the maritime provinces in relation to different farm products, dairy produce being one. The situation is, I understand, that at certain times the price prevailing in the maritime provinces is the Montreal price plus the freight, and at other times under different conditions it becomes the Montreal price less the freight. Double the freight for that distance amounts to quite a margin. An effort is being made at the present time I believe, largely on account of the fact that dairy products are being marketed by the board in Great Britain; that is, we are simply making agreements with Great Britain and taking practically all the cheese for the time being out of Ontario and Quebec and sending it to Britain. Therefore there is a tendency for that to have some effect in t'he maritimes because they are not producing as much cheese as they consume; their cheese is not entering in any great volume into the export, and there is a situation that they wish to clear up for themselves. If they desire to set up a board, no doubt our board will try to cooperate with theirs in seeking to bring about proper conditions.
Does the minimum price cover dairy products sold by a farmer?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The minimum price is set for creamery butter graded to certain grades, but the fact that there is a minimum price for creamery butter will have an effect on the price of dairy butter.
Does a person building a cheese or butter factory have to have a permit from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I do not think a
creamery operator has to have a permit. There are regulations with regard to marketing, but I do not think it is necessary to get a permit to start.

The reason why I asked the question is this. A creamery company started to build a creamery near Fredericton a year ago. They were refused a permit by the department of agriculture of New Brunswick. They were buying cream and milk in that county and shipping it all the way to Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, to manufacture, and they were refused a permit to build a creamery in the town of Devon just across the river from Fredericton. Can a provincial department of agriculture refuse a permit to anyone to build a butter factory or a factory of any kind?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It would depend upon the provincial legislation. I am not sufficiently familiar with the laws of New Brunswick to say whether there is power to do that. While they have not had legislation in Saskatchewan, there was some indirect control over creameries due to the fact that they have the cooperatives which pretty well cover the province. For some time they did try to prevent the building of two creameries in one district, and they may have some similar regulations in New Brunswick. I am not familiar with that.

I have in my hand a copy of The People's Weekly, published in Edmonton, dated May 10, 1941, which contains a photograph of a number of apples headed "Government dumps unsold apples." Below this photograph I find this article:
Growers not permitted to give them away in B.C.
On April 16th last 5,000 boxes of tasty Delicious apples were taken from cold storage at Oliver, B.C., and dumped on the authority of the dominion government, which pays eighty per cent of the average price for the quantities which the grower cannot sell.
I checked up in the parliamentary library and found that one of the weekly newspapers published in the fruit district made reference to a similar article which appeared in the Vancouver press. It has not been categorically denied that this was done. Has the minister anything to say as to whether this is an accurate photograph of apples which were dumped and, if so, would he explain the policy under which that was done?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have not the article before me, and I do not know exactly to what it refers. I know that for the last two seasons we have had agreements, and that we are entering into another agreement this year, under which the government of Canada assists the apple growers on account of the fact that since the beginning of the war they have not been able to market their apples in Britain. In the first year of the war Britain
Supply-Agriculture

did take some of our apples, but none have been exported since that time. The first year we canned some of the surplus; we dehydrated some, principally in Nova Scotia, and we entered into an arrangement with the apple growers of British Columbia whereby we agreed to pay them a certain price per box for any apples they had left the following March; and it was under that arrangement that some of the apples-I am not sure that the number stated is correct-had to be taken over by the federal government at the end of March of this year. I presume that is what is referred to in that article.

Would the minister complete the picture? This article goes on to say:
Sponsored by the Vancouver board of trade,
72.000	apples were given away to school children last January. The gesture might well have been repeated.
The article also states:
A resident of Oliver, in sending along the above picture of some of the dumped apples, states, "They are lovely apples, many of them wrapped, but they are not even allowed to give them away. The growers have not had 'apple money' for a long time."
Would the minister state whether or not those apples were thrown away?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I understand that some apples were dumped out, but I can assure the hon. member that while a few of the apples in the boxes might have been good, they were not dumped out generally if they were fit for use. Some of the apples in the boxes might have been fit for consumption, but generally speaking any that were thrown out could not be used. As a matter of fact, the year before, we shipped a great many boxes of apples to the prairies, out of the quantity we had to take delivery of, and gave them away; and I am quite sure that if these apples had been good, they would have been given to somebody.

The article states that
5.000	boxes were dumped, and the photograph would indicate that a great many of those apples were in good condition. Many of the people on the prairies have not been able to buy apples for a long time, and apples have not been issued to people on relief.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is what I am trying to say; I do not believe the article is exactly correct. They must have been poor apples, or they would have been shipped to somebody.

Could the minister
say what quantity has been dumped? Apparently it was quite a large quantity.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The contract is not
completed yet, and we have not the final figures. Therefore I would not care even to try to guess at how many were unfit for use and were dumped.

As I understand it,
the minister does not question the accuracy of this article-

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I neither question it
nor agree with it.	I did not write the
article, and consequently I do not know whether it is right or wrong.

In this connection I
have a letter from one of my constituents which offers a suggestion in connection with getting rid of the wheat surplus:
I happen to be the local attendance officer for this school district. By the teacher's report there were three children kept home during the month because their parents had no flour to bake bread for their lunches.
What applies to flour certainly would apply to fruit. I have before me a copy of "Farmers in a Changing World," the year book for 1940 of the United States department of agriculture. Has the minister given consideration to anything similar to the stamp plan in the United States which, under the direction of Milo Perkins, has been used to dispose of a number of surplus commodities? This article states:
Millions of low income people would eat more of these surpluses if they had the chance. The stamp plan is designed to give some of them that chance. It kills four birds with one stone. (1) The farmer sells the so-called surplus through (2) the grocer, who thereby increases his business, to (3) low income families, whose health is bettered by eating these foods; and finally (4) the nation gains all around through partially solving an acute economic problem and lifting the standards of health at the point where they are usually lowest.
Has the minister given consideration to a plan of that kind in order to dispose of a considerable quantity of our surplus wheat and fruit, in view of the fact that we are not likely to be able to sell large quantities of Canadian fruit in the European markets for the next few years?
And potatoes.

Yes, and potatoes,
because last winter there were parts of Canada without adequate supplies of potatoes.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We have gone very

and British Columbia and shipped to the prairies for distribution. We did that not only with fruit but also with fish, cheese and many other products. Then I think it was only two years ago that we bought up the extra butter in the months of June and July and gave it to people in cities right across Canada. As a matter of fact, the plan which has been followed in the United States has been adapted to the needs of this country. We have not the large centres of population they have in the United States, and therefore could not follow exactly the plan they have followed; but as a government we have bought, up food and given it to people who otherwise could not have obtained it. We have bought fruits and vegetables of different kinds and shipped them into some of the very areas from which letters such as the one read by my hon. friend might have come.
But not under the stamp plan.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Under a similar plan. All the stamp plan means is that these people go on to the market when they think the price is too low and buy up the surplus, which is delivered by means of stamps to unemployed people in the cities. We did not use stamps, but we gave them certificates which they could take and get butter with. It was much the same principle.
